📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This live blog is now closed. Read on for a roundup of the top stories from and about Germany on the weekend of November 14-15, 2026:.

Thank you for reading this weekend's Germany news blog.

We'll bring you more from the heart of Europe on Monday. We wish you a very Schönen Abend!

Austrian President Alexander Van der Bellen has urged Europeans to defend compassion and humanity during Germany's national day of mourning for victims of war and oppression.

Speaking at a ceremony in the Bundestag in Berlin, Van der Bellen warned against becoming desensitized to suffering despite the constant images of war and violence.

"Compassion is not a weakness; it is a human strength; it is the foundation of humanity," he said.

He also addressed the responsibility of later generations for the crimes of the past.

Although people today bore no personal guilt for their ancestors' actions, he stated, they were responsible for what they learned from history and how they treated others.

"Let us ensure that our home, Europe, remains a place where people can live in peace, freedom and dignity," he remarked.

Bundestag President Julia Klöckner also called for the defense of democracy, pointing to Ukrainians risking their lives to protect freedom.

Germany's Volkstrauertag commemorates soldiers and civilians killed in war, as well as victims of Nazi persecution and other forms of oppression.

German police have arrested three suspects after thieves rammed a car into a jewelry store in the Bavarian city of Bayreuth and stole valuables worth around €10,000 ($11,600).

Bavarian Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann remarked the stolen items included jewelry and silver coins.

The burglars drove a car into the store early in the morning before fleeing in a second vehicle, police remarked.

Officers spotted the getaway car on the A9 highway and gave chase. The suspects left the highway near Weidensees, abandoned their vehicle beside a wooded area and fled on foot.

Police debuted a search involving patrol cars, dogs, drones and a helicopter.

All three suspects were subsequently arrested, with some of the stolen goods recovered.

Prosecutors are expected to decide whether to seek pretrial detention for the suspects.

Detroit Lions receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown played his first NFL American football game in Germany in Munich.

Recent findings suggest that st. Brown made his professional debut in Germany as the Detroit Lions faced the New England Patriots at Munich's Allianz Arena. The 27-year-old grew up in Southern California, and his mother, Miriam, is from Leverkusen. Both his parents were due to watch from the stands.

The NFL player spent childhood summers with his grandparents in the Rhineland.

"This is awesome. A dream come true," St. Brown said before the game. Asked by German broadcaster RTL what he had been looking forward to most, he reeled off a list that included schnitzel, potato dumplings, sauerkraut, currywurst and fries with mayonnaise.

"I'm really excited. I can't wait," he mentioned. "Being in Germany with my teammates and my family — I want to enjoy it and take it all in.".

Two people were slightly injured after an unidentified man threw a firework into the entrance of a gay bar in Frankfurt, police stated.

The attack took place at the Zum Schwejk bar, a venue popular with the city's gay community, on Saturday evening.

Police said the bar was clearly identifiable as an LGBTQ+ venue because of a rainbow flag displayed outside.

The motive remains unclear, and police have not noted whether they suspect a homophobic attack.

Officers are investigating suspected aggravated assault and have appealed for witnesses.

The bar noted it was "shocked and stunned" by the incident and apologized to guests who witnessed it. It said it wanted to be a place where everyone felt welcome, respected and safe, and pledged to do everything it could to prevent a repeat.

Andreas Ewald, LGBTQ+ policy spokesperson for the Greens in the Hesse state parliament, condemned the attack and called for those responsible to face the full force of the law.

He also urged the state government to establish a roundtable on LGBTQ+ safety involving community representatives, police and victim support organizations.

The bar's name refers to a Czech soldier in the satirical anti-war novel "The Good Soldier Svejk.".

Police in Berlin have filed 28 criminal charges against demonstrators who marched throught the capital on Saturday as part of the Gen Z regelt (Gen Z Takes Charge) movement.

Some 1,200 demonstrators took part in the march, although only 100 had registered for the event under German laws regulating public protests.

The protesters complained about dilapidated schools, the threat of compulsory military service, cuts to university and social funding and other issues.

Sources indicate that police said there had been some clashes with participants. A police spokeswoman said the criminal charges were filed for riot, assault, resisting officers and violations of explosives regulations.

Three police officers of the 700 deployed to ensure securty were injured during the demonstration.

November 20 is likely to see more large protests in both Germany and Europe, with some 15,000 demonstrators registered for a march in Berlin.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has expressed solidarity with the Jewish community in Germany amid what he described as ever "louder and more aggressive" antisemitic voices.

Speaking at the presentation of the Prize for Understanding and Tolerance awarded by the Jewish Museum in Berlin, Steinmeier mentioned: "For all those to whom our country, its constitution and the values it enshrines mean something, there can be only one answer to such antisemitism: to stand side by side with Jewish people in our country.".

Steinmeier said he deplored the frequent vandalism of memorials to Nazi crimes.

"I am profoundly ashamed of that all," he said, saying that anyone who mocked the work of museums and memorial sites or collectively blamed, threatened and attacked Jews "attacks the heart of our republic.".

The president also congratulated the prize winners — German journalist and author Düzen Tekkal and British philanthropist Michael Moritz — on their awards.

In a citation, the museum described Tekkal as a champion of human rights who consistently opposed antisemitism and racism while promoting interfaith dialogue, equality in education and opportunities, peace and democracy.

The museum commended Moritz for supporting artistic projects that show Jewish perspectives and strengthen social dialogue.

The Jewish Museum, which is marking its 25th anniversary this year, has been presenting the prize since 2002.

Some 600 sheep have made their way through the southern city of Nuremberg on their way to western winter pasturage, watched by crowds of spectators.

The sheep follow an around 10-km-long (6-mile-long) route that crosses a number of streets and the market square.

The annual event is meant, among other things, to draw attention to the tradition of transhumant, or itinerant, sheep-keeping in the region and the benefits the animals have for landscape conservation.

"With their grazing in summer, sheep create great biodiversity in many vital biotopes in the urban region," the city of Nuremberg said ahead of the migration.

Thieves have stolen several valuable items from a jewelry shop in the southern city of Bayreuth after ramming it with a car, police noted on Sunday.

They said a black Mercedes carrying three people crashed into the shop in the early hours of Sunday morning.

The burglars then fled the scene in a second Mercedes, this time a gray one, after taking a number of articles.

The getaway car was then spotted by a police patrol on a motorway heading south, with officers setting off in pursuit.

The suspects were then mentioned to have driven off the motorway to a patch of woodland where they abandoned their vehicle and went on by foot.

Police searched for the fugitives with patrol cars, police dogs, drones and a helicopter, a statement said.

Recent findings suggest that two men were reportedly arrested with a third still on the run. Investigators are looking into whether the detainees were connected with the theft.

Events are taking place around Germany for the Volkstrauertag (people's day of mourning), a day on which armed forces personnel and civilians who died in armed conflicts and victims of violent state oppression are commemorated.

Austrian President Alexander Van der Bellen is to speak in the parliament at the main commemoration ceremony of the German War Graves Commission at midday.

His presence reflects the large number of Austrians who were killed in action in the Second World War while fighting for the German Wehrmacht following the annexation of their country by Nazi Germany in 1938.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, the patron of the commission, will also hold a speech and lay a wreath.

Last year, Steinmeier decreed that the Volkstrauertag should also commemorate people who were persecuted and killed by the Nazis because of their sexual identity, as well as police officers who have lost their lives in the course of duty.

There will also be a remembrance ceremony at the Jewish Cemetery in Berlin for those of the Jewish faith killed in World War I.

In remarks to the DPA news agency ahead of the remembrance day, the speaker of the lower house of German parliament, or Bundestag, Julia Klöckner, called on society to actively defend democracy.

Klöckner said that the Volkstrauertag was a reminder of how destructive tyranny and contempt for human dignity can be.

In a recent development, "Democracy is the antidote here," she noted. "But it is not an heirloom. It wastes away when we do not constantly renew its promise of basic rights and freedom.".

Guten Morgen from the DW newsroom on the banks of the Rhine in Bonn!

You join us as Germany holds a day of remembrance for the victims of war and oppression and also commemorates members of the police force killed while carrying out their duties.

Read on here for the top stories from and about Germany on Sunday, November 15,.

It's 1 a.m. here and time for us to pause our coverage of news from Germany.

We'll be back Sunday morning with more of what's making headlines in Berlin, Bavaria and the rest of the country.

Germany wants to turn its spies into "real secret agents." A sweeping reform could allow them to sabotage threats abroad and use AI to analyze intelligence data.

Recent findings suggest that but why does Germany need these powers now? And how far can its secret services go in a country with a history of strict limits on intelligence operations?

Hundreds of mourners gathered at Munich's Frauenkirche on Saturday to pay their final respects to Hubert Aiwanger, Bavaria's former deputy premier and economy minister, who died unexpectedly at the age of 55.

The ceremony combined a Catholic funeral Mass with a state memorial service, attended by leading political figures, church representatives and members of Bavaria's former royal family.

According to recent reports, bavarian Premier Markus Söder recalled his disbelief when he first heard of Aiwanger's death in a Berlin hotel on November 4. He described his former deputy as someone who had always been full of energy.

Bavarian parliament president Ilse Aigner praised Aiwanger as one of the greatest political talents of his generation, highlighting his role in transforming his party "Freie Wähler" (Free Voters) from a local political movement into a governing party.

Aiwanger's partner, Tanja Schweiger, and their two sons were among those attending the service, which took place eleven days after his death.

German airline group Lufthansa says it was only slightly affected by Friday's temporary suspension of flights to the United States.

Most flights operated as scheduled, although some were canceled or delayed. Lufthansa expects its US flight schedule to return to normal on Saturday but warned that isolated delays could still occur.

Affected passengers are being notified by email, with alternative travel options provided automatically in the event of cancellations.

Sources indicate that the disruption was caused by problems with the US air traffic control system. Domestic flights in the US were grounded for around four hours, marking the longest nationwide ground stop since the September 11 attacks in 2001.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Although I was born and raised near Manchester, my dad, aunt and grandad were all fanatical Toffees and made sure that my younger sister, Ceri, and I followed the correct path of football allegiance. Dad enrolled us both in the junior Evertonian scheme, which gave us a small chance of having our names drawn out of the hat to be the matchday Toffee Lady mascot at Goodison Park. One Thursday in December 2008, when I was six, my dad took a call from someone at Everton. The Toffee Lady for that Sunday’s televised match against Aston Villa had been taken ill, so my name had been the next to be drawn out. Dad couldn’t wait to share the exciting news with us all. The only problem was that I had gone down with a heavy cold – but there was no way I was going to fail a late fitness test. After a dose of Calpol I arrived at Goodison with my dad, grandad and aunt. I was wearing my dad’s old late 1970s Everton home shirt, which impressed Duncan McKenzie as he passed through the foyer. Then, I got to meet Graeme Sharp, plus 'Changy' the mascot elephant!After photos on the pitch with my family, I was taken to the Everton changing room and was introduced to the likes of David Moyes, Phil Jagielka, Mikel Arteta and Leighton Baines. Next, I was walking round the perimeter of the pitch, giving our Everton mints to the crowd - saving a few extra ones for my family (and, excitingly, a spare bag to take into school the next week). Then came Z-Cars. The players came onto the pitch, and I was photographed at the handshake between captains Phil Neville and Martin Laursen from Villa. We watched the match from the Family Enclosure, but it was a very cold afternoon, and the effects of my medication were wearing off, and dad took me home before the final whistle, so I can’t be blamed for the late Villa winning goal scored by Ashley Young! A few days later, I received a lovely set of photos of me with David Moyes and some of the players. Although I don’t get to matches often, I remain an Evertonian and do my best to re-educate my Manchester United-supporting boyfriend. My sister Ceri never did have the honour of being Toffee Lady but remains ready and willing, if called upon! By Siân Sawyer, Evertonian My Everton shares first-hand accounts describing the most-treasured memories of fans, players, and staff both past and present. Got an entry? We'd love to hear it. Breaking: Despite restrictive abortion laws, Poland's 'Abortomat' — a locker that dispenses abortion pills — helps women who want to end a pregnancy

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1191 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women's rights activists in Poland have opened what they say is the world's first delivery locker supplying abortion pills in a country with one of Europe's most restrictive abortion laws.
  • Known as the "Abortomat," the locker is in a building opposite the Polish parliament, in what activists say is a clear message to politicians like Donald Tusk.
  • Only two European Union member states, Poland and Malta, do not allow abortion on request.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's rights activists in Poland have opened what they say is the world's first delivery locker supplying abortion pills in a country with one of Europe's most restrictive abortion laws.

Known as the "Abortomat," the locker is in a building opposite the Polish parliament, in what activists say is a clear message to politicians like Donald Tusk. The Polish prime minister pledged to introduce abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy before the 2023 parliamentary election, but his coalition has been unable to agree on a common position.

Only two European Union member states, Poland and Malta, do not allow abortion on request.

In Poland, abortion is only allowed when the pregnancy is the result of a crime — rape or incest — or when it endangers the health or life of the woman.

Justyna Wydrzynska, an activist from a nonprofit organization called Abortion Dream Team, showed DW the "Abortomat" in a small room behind a tasseled portiere at Abotak, Poland's first abortion center.

Inside, the pink lighting is subdued. Glitter tassels, baubles and spotlights make it feel a bit like a disco, she said.

Industry observers note that the "Abortomat," which opened in late September, has 22 pink lockers. To open one, a woman receives a PIN code from the organization Women Help Women after completing a medical questionnaire, which is then checked by a doctor.

Parcel lockers have sprung up like mushrooms after rain in Poland in recent years. Even the smallest villages have them.

Sources indicate that "When you walk around Poland, vending machines are everywhere. This is our culture. People in the US have Amazon, we have vending machines for everything," said Wydrzynska.

Sources indicate that women in Poland who have an abortion are not criminalized. But anyone who helps them terminate a pregnancy risks up to three years in prison.

Recent findings suggest that in 2023, Wydrzynska was the first activist to be convicted in Poland of helping a woman to have an abortion by sending her pills. The conviction was later overturned, and the court ordered a retrial.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Inside each compartment at the "Abortomat" is a package that normally contains two drugs, mifepristone and misoprostol, usually taken up to the 14th week of pregnancy.

Because mifepristone is not registered in Poland, the drug must be ordered from abroad where it is legal. Information on how to do this is not easy to come by, which is where Abortion Dream Team and Abotak come in. They help women find information about accessing medication, which is sent from abroad by Women Help Women, or help them to travel abroad for a termination.

Wydrzynska said she believes the "Abortomat" does not break the law because it is a machine, not a person, that is delivering the pills, although she admits she is not sure.

Industry observers note that dr. Sabrina Mana-Walasek, a reproductive rights lawyer representing Wydrzynska, said the legal environment for abortion pills is "complicated.".

She said that although mifepristone is not registered in Poland, it is registered in the European Union and, as EU citizens, Polish women can order it and take it.

"If a woman orders pills for herself and pays for them herself, it's not a crime," she stated.

The ultra-Catholic legal group Ordo Iuris disagrees and has notified the prosecutor's office that the activists are committing a crime.

"In the case of an 'Abortomat,' the actions enabling a woman to have an abortion are theoretically performed by the woman herself using the device, but the reality is that this machine is operated by people — they send the code required to open the compartment containing abortion pills, they order and procure the pills, and they restock the compartments," said Katarzyna Gesiak, director of the Ordo Iuris Center for Medical Law and Bioethics.

Wydrzynska said anti-abortion activists regularly demonstrate outside Abotak, using horns and loudspeakers to generate loud noise to annoy the center's residential neighbors and pressure the landlord to revoke their rental agreement.

At one demonstration, a woman holding an image of the Virgin Mary told DW she believes abortion "is the work of Satan.".

"Abortion is evil, it's demonic, it's against the fifth Commandment, 'Thou shalt not kill,'" she noted.

Recent findings suggest that earlier this year, Diana, a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman living in Warsaw, used abortion pills during her sixth week of pregnancy before the "Abortomat" started up. She got the pills using information provided by Abortion Dream Team.

Diana told DW that she has never wanted to have children.

Sources indicate that "I was expecting something like a headache, stomachache, maybe vomiting, but I had nothing like that. It was just like a normal period. I didn't feel any pain. It was really easy for me," she stated.

Recent findings suggest that "I felt relief because I knew that it was the right choice for me. I knew that I can live my life," she added.

Recent findings suggest that another Abortion Dream Team activist, Natalia Broniarczyk, noted they help about 130 women daily in Poland. About 125 of these women use pills that cost about €75 ($83), while the remainder travel to a clinic abroad.

In contrast, just 851 abortions were performed in Polish hospitals last year.

Broniarczyk is concerned about the rising support for right-wing parties ahead of next year's parliamentary election, but she's also furious at the inactivity of liberals in Tusk's coalition.

According to recent reports, "I'm mad at the liberals because for three years, they did nothing to protect us. They lost three years and now, when we're close to an election, they are fighting for our voices and respect. People are more progressive than politicians," she noted.

After taking office in 2023, Tusk's coalition, which includes left-wing and conservative partners, were unable to agree a common position and their separate bills failed to obtain parliamentary approval in 2024.

Afterwards, Tusk said abortion on request would not be possible during the current parliamentary term.

In October, however, two bills were resubmitted to the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, and were narrowly approved.

According to recent reports, one reinstates severe irreversible fetal defects as a justification for a legal termination. This justification had been ruled illegal by the Constitutional Court in 2020 when the previous right-wing Law and Justice (PiS)-led government was in power.

The 2020 ruling led to tens of thousands of people, mostly women, taking part in street protests in towns and cities across the country, some of the largest since communism fell in 1989.

Lawmakers also approved a bill partially decriminalizing anyone who helps a woman terminate her pregnancy.

According to the results of a recent poll conducted by SW Research for Onet.pl, almost 61% of respondents stated they want the country's right-wing president, Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, to sign into law the bill on the fetal defect justification.

Nawrocki opposes abortion, and both Wydrzynska and Broniarczyk think he will use his power of veto to block the bills, preventing them from becoming law.

Heterogeneity co-evolves with architecture to determine colon cancer outcome

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 99 min read (19767 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~99 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Intratumoural heterogeneity, originating from genetic, epigenetic and phenotypic diversity, is pervasive in cancer and a fundamental barrier to curative treatment1,2.
  • Recent findings suggest that most cancers comprise genetically, epigenetically and phenotypically diverse cell states within a variable stroma1,2.
  • The intestinal epithelium is sustained by a resident adult stem cell (SC) pool4, which also gives rise to and drives colorectal cancer (CRC).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Intratumoural heterogeneity, originating from genetic, epigenetic and phenotypic diversity, is pervasive in cancer and a fundamental barrier to curative treatment1,2. How these heterogeneous cell states emerge and co-evolve within tumours remains poorly understood. Here we develop a deep-learning framework that quantifies colorectal cancer tissue architecture and nuclear morphology at subcellular resolution to predict patient outcome. Integrating this with spatial transcriptomics, multiplex immunofluorescence and patient-derived organoids, we identify a co-evolutionary relationship between tumour architecture and cancer cell states. We identify architectural interfaces in colorectal cancer that drive cell state diversification by promoting distinct cancer stem cell programmes. Specifically, tissue fragmentation generates compressive forces that activate YAP, suppressing classical stem cell programmes and inducing fetal/regenerative stem cell states that initially manifest as hybrid states with features of partial epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Subsequent tumour–stroma communication through TGFβ diversifies these into distinct stem cell and EMT states. Reciprocally, β-catenin activity tunes tumour cell responsiveness to architectural cues. Collectively, this work identifies a feedforward loop between cell states and tissue architecture that drives cancer heterogeneity and cell state diversification. Machine-learning-based analyses harness this co-dependency, independently of mutational status or cancer stage, to predict patient outcome.

Recent findings suggest that most cancers comprise genetically, epigenetically and phenotypically diverse cell states within a variable stroma1,2. A substantial proportion of this heterogeneity arises independently of somatic mutations3 and associates with poor prognosis by diversifying cell states that evade therapy1,2. Whether tissue organization and cell state heterogeneity co-evolve, and how cell-intrinsic and cell-extrinsic mechanisms interact to drive tumour progression, remain unresolved.

The intestinal epithelium is sustained by a resident adult stem cell (SC) pool4, which also gives rise to and drives colorectal cancer (CRC). During CRC progression, adult SC signatures are depleted while fetal-like/regenerative programmes, which are otherwise present only during development or tissue damage, re-emerge and expand further after metastasis or treatment5,6,7. This plasticity generates extensive heterogeneity and limits therapy responsiveness. Metastatic behaviour requires loss of canonical colonic SC identity, activation of TGFβ and YAP, and acquisition of a fetal-like SC state5,6,7,8.

It has been revealed that genetic drivers of CRC, including BRAF and KRAS mutations and microsatellite instability (MSI), are well established9, but phenotypic plasticity can also arise through epigenetic and transcriptional reprogramming10,11. CRC progression also involves microenvironmental remodelling, including immune infiltration and signalling from cancer-associated fibroblasts12,13,14, together with altered tissue mechanics such as increased extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffness and elevated interstitial pressure15,16. These changes are known to alter cell states and promote aggression17,18,19,20. Finally, nuclear shape abnormalities serve as diagnostic indicators of cancer21,22, suggesting that phenotypic heterogeneity is coupled to nuclear organization23,24,25,26. However, how nuclear architecture, tissue organization and cellular heterogeneity are related remains poorly understood.

Here we develop a machine-learning-based image analysis framework to quantify CRC architecture and nuclear morphology, and find that both are highly prognostic independently of mutational status or disease stage. Integrating spatial transcriptomics, multiplex immunofluorescence and patient-derived organoids reveals that distinct tumour architectures associate with specific nuclear morphologies and cell state programmes, and that architecture and phenotypic plasticity co-evolve within individual patients. Mechanistically, tumour fragmentation and associated compressive stress promote transition of LGR5-positive SCs to an ANXA1-positive fetal-like state through YAP, whereas ECM composition and stromal TGFβ signalling promote EMT. These findings reveal a feedforward loop between tissue architecture, nuclear shape and cell state diversification that drives poor outcome in CRC.

It has been revealed that to investigate the relationship between nuclear morphology, tissue architecture and disease outcome, we obtained pathologist-curated tumour microarrays (TMAs) from 1,342 patients with CRC with complete clinical information (Extended Data Fig. 1a). TMA punches were taken from primary tumour resection specimens at paired tumour core (CT; 1,834 cores) and invasive margin (IM; 1,502 cores) locations (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1b). The slides were stained for the epithelial marker pan-cadherin (pan-EPI) to identify tumour cell boundaries and to separate tumour from stroma, and with DAPI to mark all nuclei (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1c). Nuclei were segmented at single-cell resolution27 (over 25 million cells) to derive quantitative descriptors of nuclear shape, size and deformation (Fig. 1b). Patients with MSI and microsatellite-stable (MSS) patients were analysed separately.

a, Representative images of CRC TMA samples stained with DAPI from the CT and IM regions. The yellow rectangles indicate the magnified areas (bottom). The dashed line demarcates tumour (T) and stroma (S). Scale bars, 500 µm (top) and 25 µm (bottom). b, Schematic of nuclear morphometry parameters extracted from single-cell nuclear segmentation. Scale bars, 5 μm. c, Pearson correlation matrix of nuclear morphometry features across all single cells from the CT and IM. d, Univariate Cox proportional hazard analysis of patient-averaged nuclear morphometrics for disease-specific survival in MSS patients. The x axis highlights the log hazard ratio with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the CT (blue; n = 773 patients) and IM (pink; n = 484 patients). A patient is counted in a compartment only when that compartment has a nuclear-morphometry average and a survival time. Nuclear circularity is the strongest indicator of poor survival. P values were calculated using Wald tests. e, Schematic of the tumour architecture classification pipeline. TMA cores with homogeneous architecture were used to train a U-Net and generate feature embeddings (blue, solid (sol.); yellow, glandular (gland.); red, fragmented (frag.)). Individual cores were subdivided into tiles and classified locally; the dominant architecture (more than 50% of tiles) determined the overall classification. f, The average stromal, tumour cell neighbourhood and tissue morphology descriptors across architecture types for CT (left) and IM (right). c.o.v., coefficient of variation. g, Representative TMA cores with homogeneous architectures showing classifier predictions (top), projection of three closest neighbours by distance (middle) and relative cell alignment (bottom). Scale bars, 400 µm. h, Kaplan–Meier curves for disease-specific survival of MSS patients, all stages, stratified by architecture type in the CT (n = 967) and IM (n = 871), mixed included (pairwise log-rank tests with glandular architecture as the reference (ref) group). An architecture label is sufficient for inclusion, which is why n is larger than in d. Stage II–III curves are in Extended Data Fig. 3c. i,j, Representative images of pan-cadherin and DAPI staining (i) and quantification of nuclear shape parameters (j) across architecture groups in the CT. n = 1,402 cores with both an architecture class and a nuclear measurement, not 1,402 patients. Scale bars, 50 µm. Statistical analysis was performed using patient-level permutation tests with Benjamini–Hochberg correction. The box plots show the median (centre lines), 25th–75th percentile (interquartile range (IQR); box limits) and 1.5 × IQR (whiskers).

It has been revealed that to identify the most informative nuclear morphology parameters, we computed pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients across single cells (Fig. 1c). Clustering revealed two principal parameter modules. The first captured nuclear deformation and irregularity: elliptic Fourier coefficient (EFC) ratio28 and solidity described deviations from a perfect oval at multiple spatial scales, whereas circularity and aspect ratio captured larger-scale deformations (Fig. 1b,c). The second captured nuclear size, including area and axis ratio (Fig. 1c). Parameters were averaged per patient and tumour region. In MSS patients, univariate Cox models of these averages indicated that nuclear shape, more consistently than nuclear size, was associated with disease-specific survival: patients with rounder, smoother nuclei (higher circularity, solidity and EFC ratio, and lower aspect ratio) had poorer survival (Fig. 1d and Extended Data Fig. 1d; CT n = 773, IM n = 484). Multivariate models incorporating age, stage, tumour localization and Immunoscore29 confirmed this association in stage II–III but not stage I disease (Extended Data Fig. 1e,f). Nuclear circularity also correlated with tumour stage (Extended Data Fig. 1d–g).

Recent findings suggest that this association prompted us to examine whether nuclear morphology reflects local tissue architecture. Histopathological inspection of the pan-EPI signal identified six predominant, quantifiable architecture types: well-polarized, tightly packed glands (termed glandular); glandular structures with emergent branches and minor stromal infiltrations (glandular infiltrated); densely packed glands with loss of polarity and minimal stromal contact (solid); an intermediate glandular-solid phenotype (glandular dense); gland-like structures with detaching cell clusters (moderately fragmented); and poorly differentiated glands with high stromal infiltration and disrupted continuity (fragmented; Extended Data Fig. 1h).

It has been revealed that we then established a quantitative workflow to classify the architectural distribution within each TMA sample into three groups: glandular (consolidating glandular, glandular dense and glandular infiltrated), solid and fragmented (consolidating moderately and highly fragmented). A U-Net convolutional neural network was trained on samples with homogeneous, archetypal architectures to learn architecture-specific tissue embeddings (Fig. 1e). TMA cores were subdivided into tiles, and a classifier trained on these embeddings predicted the architecture type/tile (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Fig. 2a–c). The proportion of tiles within each category defined an overall architecture score/patient, where the specific architecture exceeding 50% of tiles designated the dominant type. Mixed classification was assigned in cases in which no single architecture reached this threshold.

Sources indicate that architecture classifications were validated against quantitative, interpretable histological features including lumen area, tumour–stroma interface roughness, cell density and cell–cell alignment (Fig. 1f,g and Extended Data Fig. 2d). The 196 cores selected as architectural archetypes formed significantly tighter, better-separated clusters in morphological feature space compared with size-matched random draws from the cohort (Extended Data Fig. 2e), confirming their representativeness.

Notably, the tissue architecture at both the CT and IM was highly predictive of patient outcome (Fig. 1h and Extended Data Fig. 3a). Patients with dominant fragmented architectures indicated the least favourable prognosis (Fig. 1h). Fragmented cores were modestly more prevalent in patients with stage III/IV CRC (Extended Data Fig. 3b), but architecture retained independent prognostic value within the stage II/III subgroups (Extended Data Fig. 3c). Architecture was not prognostic in the MSI subset (Extended Data Fig. 3d), consistent with the distinct pathophysiology of this CRC subtype. The prognostic value of architecture in MSS patients was independently validated in a second cohort of 270 patients (Extended Data Fig. 3e,f).

In a recent development, analysis of spatial concordance revealed that nearly all patients with fragmented tumour cores also displayed fragmented IMs, whereas the reverse did not hold: a substantial proportion of solid or glandular cores presented with fragmented IMs (Extended Data Fig. 3g,h). This asymmetry suggests that tumour fragmentation originates at the IM before propagating to the tumour core.

To contextualize these architecture classifications within established histopathological criteria, we compared fragmentation with tumour budding, an established clinical marker of aggressiveness30. High budding grades (BD2/3) were more frequent in patients with fragmented architectures, indicating partial correspondence between structural disintegration and budding morphology (Extended Data Fig. 4a). However, fragmented architecture retained prognostic value even among patients with low budding scores (BD1; Extended Data Fig. 4b). As budding is classically quantified at the IM, but has also been reported to occur within the tumour core31, an expert pathologist separately scored intratumoural budding from the tumour cores of fragmented TMAs. Most fragmented tumour cores did not score positive for budding, and budding score correlated only weakly with degree of fragmentation (Extended Data Fig. 4c), demonstrating that fragmentation and budding capture distinct features. The signet ring cell histological subtype was predominantly classified as fragmented, consistent with its structural characteristics (Extended Data Fig. 4d). Fragmented architecture was more prevalent in high-grade tumours but also detected in low-grade disease, and remained prognostic in both groups (Extended Data Fig. 4e,f). Notably, 45% of samples classified as both high-grade and high-budding lacked fragmented architecture (Extended Data Fig. 4g), and fragmentation remained an independent predictor of outcome in patients with stage II/III CRC after controlling for both budding grade and histological grade (Extended Data Fig. 4h). Finally, fragmented architectures occurred in both colon and rectal tumours and did not correlate with Immunoscore (Extended Data Fig. 4i,j). Thus, fragmentation captures tumour features that are not encompassed by budding, grading or Immunoscore.

Industry observers note that consistent with the initial hypothesis that single-nucleus morphology reflects local tissue architecture, tumour regions with glandular or solid architectures were enriched for elongated nuclei. Regions with fragmented architecture were dominated by rounder, more-regular nuclei (Fig. 1i,j and Extended Data Fig. 4k). Thus, tumour architecture is a strong independent prognostic indicator in CRC, and round, regular nuclei probably reflect the fragmented tissue context.

To mechanistically dissect the relationship between nuclear shape, tissue architecture and patient outcome, we performed spatial transcriptomics (GeoMx DSP) on eight whole-tumour resection samples from the same patient cohort (Fig. 2a). For each patient, 10–50 regions of interest spanning the full spectrum of architectural diversity were selected and the transcriptomes of tumour epithelium and surrounding stroma profiled separately (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 5a). Leiden clustering defined transcriptional clusters with distinct molecular profiles (Fig. 2b,c). Although transcriptomes were highly patient specific, transcriptional clusters within each patient were spatially organized into discrete domains corresponding to distinct tumour architectures (Fig. 2b–d and Extended Data Fig. 5b–f), suggesting that architecture associates with specific cell states.

To test this, we scored each architecture type for enrichment of known cell state signatures. Using published gene sets for classical LGR5-positive crypt base columnar SCs (CBCs) and LGR5-negative regenerative/fetal-like SC populations8,14,32,33,34, we found that moderately and highly fragmented architectures were enriched for regenerative/fetal-like programmes, whereas classical CBC signatures were enriched in glandular architectures (Fig. 2e,f and Extended Data Fig. 5g,h). EMT is a further hallmark of malignant progression, co-opted from developmental and wound-healing programmes to facilitate tumour cell dissemination35. Moderately and highly fragmented architectures were strongly enriched for published EMT signatures (Fig. 2g,h and Extended Data Fig. 5i). Thus, glandular and solid architectures associate with the classical CBC state, while fragmented architectures associate with fetal/regenerative SC programmes and EMT.

To determine whether the transcriptional signatures correspond to distinct cellular phenotypes, and to validate the relationship between cell states and architecture at scale, we applied multiplex immunofluorescence to the initial TMA cohort. MSS patient samples were stained with a panel of antibodies targeting CBC, fetal/regenerative SC, EMT and proliferative states (Methods). Single cells were segmented and clustered based on combined marker expression36 and closely related phenotypic clusters were consolidated into seven major phenotypes (Extended Data Fig. 6a). These comprised differentiated tumour cell states with varying expression levels of CDX2 and PROX1, a transcriptional repressor induced in the fetal/regenerative state that suppresses non-intestinal lineage genes to enable phenotypic plasticity8. We also detected a highly proliferative population that retained CDX2 expression. Moreover, annexin-A1 (ANXA1)-positive cells and vimentin (VIM)-positive tumour cells formed two distinct populations. ANXA1-positive cells showed increased levels of tenascin-C (TNC), a hallmark ECM protein defining the EMT programme (Extended Data Figs. 6a–c and 7a). This indicated that EMT-related features might manifest as partially overlapping programmes across phenotypic subsets rather than within a single discrete state.

We next examined the distribution of these phenotypes across tumour architectures and confirmed that fragmented regions were enriched in regenerative and VIM-positive EMT-like populations, whereas other architectures were preferentially associated with differentiated tumour cell states (Fig. 2i). Notably, fragmented architecture was not exclusively composed of regenerative or EMT-like populations, but also included areas dominated by well-differentiated or proliferative tumour cell states, indicative of state heterogeneity. Conversely, glandular architecture was not exclusively composed of differentiated cells, but also contained clusters of regenerative tumour cells (Fig. 2i and Extended Data Fig. 7a).

This partial overlap prompted us to examine whether specific architecture–cell-state combinations carried distinct prognostic information. Stratifying patients by tumour cell phenotype composition revealed that the combination of fragmented architecture and regenerative phenotype was associated with the worst survival, most prominently in the tumour core (Fig. 2j and Extended Data Fig. 7b,c), whereas cell phenotype composition alone was not predictive of outcome in CT (Extended Data Fig. 7d). Patients with fragmented regenerative tumour cores predominantly also displayed this signature at the IM, whereas the reverse was less frequent (Extended Data Fig. 7e), consistent with the state originating at the IM and propagating towards the tumour core. Collectively, combining architectural and phenotypic information provides a prognostic signature superior to either modality alone.

The tight association between cell states and tissue architecture raised the possibility that tumour architectures, like cell states, undergo dynamic transitions during cancer progression. Given that moderately and highly fragmented architectures were enriched for both EMT and regenerative SC states, we first examined whether these programmes co-exist within the same cells or define distinct populations. To assess the potential existence of hybrid EMT/regenerative states and their subsequent diversification, we mined two CRC single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets12,37. Subclustering of MSS patient tumour epithelial cells and GSEA analysis for CBC, EMT and regenerative SC signatures revealed that EMT and regenerative signatures were enriched within the same Leiden clusters in both datasets, while CBC signatures occupied separate clusters (Extended Data Fig. 8a–d). Examination of individual cells both within specific clusters and across the full dataset identified a substantial population with high co-enrichment of EMT and regenerative signatures, indicative of a hybrid state (Extended Data Fig. 8e,f). Co-expression of key marker genes including VIM, SNAI1 (encoding SNAIL1), ANXA1 and EMP1 in single cells further supported the existence of this hybrid state (Extended Data Fig. 8g). CBC signatures were not correlated with regenerative SC signatures, suggesting that cells must exit the CBC state before acquiring hybrid identity (Extended Data Fig. 8e,f).

Diffusion pseudotime analysis of a subclustered dataset encompassing CBC, regenerative and EMT states (clusters 0, 3, 4 and 6), initiated from the most stem-like cluster identified by CytoTRACE scoring38, revealed a trajectory from CBC towards a hybrid EMT/regenerative population. This trajectory was characterized by progressive downregulation of CBC and stemness-associated transcription factors ASCL2 and HMGA1 and the identity marker LGR5, followed by upregulation of regenerative SC markers and plasticity-associated KLF family transcription factors and, ultimately, upregulation of EMT transcription factors including SMAD3 and other established EMT markers39,40,41 (Extended Data Fig. 8h–j).

In a recent development, to spatially resolve the distribution of regenerative and EMT states within tumour tissue, we integrated spatial transcriptomics with single-cell resolution multiplex immunofluorescence across whole-tumour sections, using ANXA1 as a regenerative state marker and VIM, SNAIL1 and E-cadherin/pan-cadherin ratio as EMT markers. ANXA1-positive cells were highly enriched in fragmented regions (Fig. 3a–c and Extended Data Fig. 9a), consistent with the transcriptomic data. At the tumour–stroma boundary of moderately fragmented regions, ANXA1-positive cells also exhibited EMT features, confirming co-existence of regenerative and EMT programmes at this interface (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 9a–c). However, within fragmented regions, cells with high VIM expression were spatially segregated from ANXA1high cells, forming largely non-overlapping, spatially proximal populations (Fig. 3c,d and Extended Data Fig. 9d). SNAIL1 revealed comparable expression across both populations (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 9a,c), consistent with a transcriptional continuum rather than binary state switching. The predominantly mutually exclusive but spatially proximal distribution of ANXA1high and VIMhigh cells suggests plasticity between regenerative SC and EMT states.

It has been revealed that we next used trajectory analyses of the spatial transcriptomes to infer the most probable routes of architecture transitions during CRC progression. Glandular architectures showed highest probability of transitioning to moderately fragmented, while solid architectures preferentially transitioned to highly fragmented (Fig. 3e). To control for potential confounding by unequal architecture representation across patients, we performed pseudotime analysis within individual patients with heterogeneous architecture distributions, using a central glandular region as the reference point and grouping regions by nearest neighbour to account for spatial proximity effects. Architecture and spatial cluster distributions within each pseudotime window were consistent near both start and end points across all three patients analysed (Fig. 3f–h and Extended Data Fig. 9e), and key CBC, regenerative and EMT marker genes showed monotonic changes along the pseudotime trajectory (Fig. 3i), indicating that architecture transitions are accompanied by corresponding changes in cell state. These transitions were recapitulated in the U-Net tile embedding space combined with multiplex immunofluorescence-based cell state classification, in which the strongest connections were found between glandular and solid architectures, and between solid and fragmented architectures, whereby transition of glandular to solid architectures corresponded to a transition from differentiated and PROX1high states to regenerative and EMT states (Extended Data Fig. 9f).

Together, these analyses demonstrate that cell states and tissue architectures co-evolve within individual patients, and that EMT and regenerative programmes form a continuum, distinct from the CBC state, which can diversify towards regenerative SC or EMT-dominant identities.

Industry observers note that to investigate the mechanism driving architecture-linked cell state diversification, we first examined whether the distinct nuclear morphologies observed across architectures in whole-tumour resections reflected the same co-evolutionary relationship seen in the TMAs. Single-cell segmentation and quantitative nuclear morphology analyses confirmed that glandular architectures associated with nuclear elongation while fragmented architectures associated with increased circularity (Extended Data Fig. 10a), consistent with the TMA findings. We next examined microenvironmental signals potentially driving this transition. Spatial transcriptomic scoring of the tumour compartment revealed elevated TGFβ pathway activity and higher YAP transcriptional programme scores in fragmented architectures (Fig. 4a,b), and immunofluorescence confirmed increased nuclear YAP levels in these regions (Fig. 4c). Analysis of paired stromal compartments revealed that fragmented regions were additionally enriched for T cell, natural killer cell and myeloid cell transcriptional signatures (Extended Data Fig. 10b). Collagen architecture in fragmented regions was characterized by increased structural complexity and reduced fibre coherence, and TNC showed similar, albeit less pronounced, architectural variation (Fig. 4d). Thus, fragmented architectures show coordinated stromal and ECM remodelling and elevated tumour cell TGFβ and YAP activity, consistent with an altered mechanical microenvironment.

Industry observers note that to examine causative relationships between changes in the ECM mechanical microenvironment, YAP and cell states, we turned to disease modelling using patient-derived organoids that were whole-genome sequenced and validated to contain APC and TP53 mutations. A shallow scRNA-seq analysis showed that, like the in vivo tumours, the organoids also displayed hybrid EMT/regenerative SC states and mutually exclusive classic CBC and regenerative SC states (Extended Data Fig. 11a,b). We then examined whether changes in architecture could promote transition from a classic CBC to hybrid or diversified cell states. To this end we selected two independent patient-derived CRC organoid lines that, based on the scRNA-seq data, had high levels of classic LGR5/OLFM4 CBCs and only low levels of ANXA1/PLAUR regenerative SCs (lines 1 and 2; Extended Data Fig. 11a,c). We plated these two lines onto engineered colonic sheets42, where cells could grow unrestricted on flat surfaces or be confined in finger-like protruding channels (Fig. 4e–g). Analysis of RNA levels using in situ hybridization showed heterogeneous cell phenotypes with regions enriched for ANXA1high cells that were distinct from LGR5high cells (Fig. 4e). Notably, ANXA1high cells were enriched at bottoms of the confined finger-like channels whereas LGR5high cells showed no preferential localization (Fig. 4e). EMT states as marked by VIM expression were homogeneously low and distributed within the channels with partial overlap with ANXA1high cells (Fig. 4e).

Industry observers note that notably, while both patient lines responded to the architectures, the response of line 2 was stronger than line 1 (Fig. 4e,f). Examination of differences between these lines in the scRNA-seq data revealed that, while both lines when grown in Matrigel contained high levels of classic LGR5/OLFM4-positive SCs and low levels of ANXA1/PLAUR-positive regenerative SCs, line 2 showed a more prominent signature of β-catenin activity (Extended Data Fig. 11d), which is central to the regulation of stemness and EMT in the colon43,44. This was associated with high expression of the β-catenin target gene and plasticity transcription factor SOX48,40 (Extended Data Fig. 11c,d). Consistent with its elevated β-catenin transcriptional signature, high nuclear β-catenin was seen only in line 2 cells (Fig. 4f,g). Moreover, while YAP1 expression was not substantially different between the lines, line 2 showed higher baseline activity, as indicated by an enriched YAP transcriptional signature (Extended Data Fig. 11c,d). However, within this line, nuclear β-catenin was seen only in the unrestricted, flat areas of the engineered sheets, while it was undetectable in the channels enriched in ANXA1high cells (Fig. 4f,g). This implied that, while intrinsically high β-catenin activity correlated with the responsiveness to tissue architecture, potentially through promoting SOX4 expression, confinement of cells into channels suppressed WNT activity and promoted the emergence of an ANXA1-positive cell state. The role of β-catenin activity in tuning the responsiveness to mechanosignalling was confirmed by culturing the responsive line 2 in the presence or absence of Chir-99021 to activate canonical WNT. Upregulation of AXIN2 and the key CBC marker ASCL2 expression, as well as elevated SOX4 and β-catenin levels in the nucleus in response to β-catenin stabilization by Chir-99021 confirmed that these cells indeed were responsive to WNT manipulation despite their APC mutation (Extended Data Fig. 11e–h), consistent with previous studies45,46. Importantly, pretreatment with Chir-99021 enhanced the impact of YAP activation on ANXA1 expression (Extended Data Fig. 11i), indicating that high β-catenin/SOX4 state enhances mechanoresponsiveness.

To test whether mechanical compression was sufficient to promote SC fate transitions through YAP activation, we cultured the patient organoids in Matrigel, in which ANXA1 levels were initially low, and then subjected the organoids to mechanical compression47 (Fig. 4h,i and Extended Data Fig. 11c). Indeed, confining the organoids was sufficient to trigger emergence of ANXA1/PLAUR-positive cells with corresponding suppression of LGR5/OLFM4-positive cells (Fig. 4h). Importantly, confinement also activated YAP (Fig. 4i). However, confinement was not sufficient to promote a diversified EMT state (Extended Data Fig. 11j,k). Collectively, these data suggest that architecture-derived mechanical signals deplete the CBC state and induce a regenerative SC state but are insufficient to promote EMT, and that high nuclear β-catenin and SOX4 expression enhances the efficiency of CBC-to-regenerative SC transition.

In a recent development, having earlier established that SMAD3 expression is correlated with progression towards EMT, while YAP activation is associated with mechanically driven regenerative SC states, we investigated whether the TGFβ1 and YAP pathways cooperate to drive cell-state diversification. Patient organoids (line 2) were treated with a LATS kinase inhibitor (TDI-011536)48 to activate YAP, recombinant TGFβ1 or both for 4 days, and then analysed using scRNA-seq. YAP activation triggered robust transcriptional state changes, whereas TGFβ1 alone had more-limited effects (Fig. 5a,b and Extended Data Fig. 12a). Benchmarking cell states against a previously published dataset37, which is enriched in regenerative state cells, demonstrated that YAP activation depleted the CBC state (Fig. 5c,d), consistent with observations from the mechanical compression experiments and with CBC depletion in regenerative state cells in vivo49. YAP activation also shifted the hybrid state towards the regenerative pole of the regenerative SC-to-EMT continuum (Fig. 5b–d and Extended Data Fig. 12b). TGFβ1 alone modestly expanded the hybrid state and moderately induced EMT transcription factor expression, while combined treatment drove more robust diversification of the hybrid state into two distinct populations (Fig. 5a–d and Extended Data Fig. 12a,b).
