Next, we performed CTCF ChIP–seq in HCASMC to prioritize disease-associated SMC enhancers that are bound by CTCF. Of all CAD disease-associated variants, 498 overlapped CTCF peaks, including 200 within accessible chromatin regions. CAD-associated variants were enriched significantly at CTCF-bound regions above permutation-based expectation (1.25-fold, P = 0.02; Extended Data Fig. 10g).

Among the top-ranking regulatory mosaics, we identified mosaic-1664, which contains the CAD-associated variant rs4887091 located within an SMC enhancer (Fig. 4c). In this mosaic, we found an 800-kb boundary loop exhibiting a strong rs4887091 genotype-dependent increase in contact strength for the alternate allele (C) relative to the reference allele (T) (Fig. 4d). Specifically, the loop strength increased in a dose-dependent manner when quantified across all samples, where there was minimal contact strength in homozygotes (T|T), moderate strength in heterozygotes (T|C, C|T) and highest strength in homozygotes (C|C) (Fig. 4e). Phased genotypes confirmed increased looping strength on the C allele (P = 3.1 × 10−3) (Fig. 4f).

To characterize the regulatory architecture of rs4887091 within mosaic-1664, we identified all genes linked to the SMC enhancer containing rs4887091: Hi-C identified a boundary loop containing ADAMTS7, MORF4L1, CHRNA3, IDH3A, ACSBG1, CIB2, SH2D7 and TBC1D2 promoters (Fig. 4d), whereas scE2G identified ADAMTS7 (the nearest gene) (Fig. 4g). Consistent with ADAMTS7 being a functional target of this regulatory element, CRISPRi Perturb–seq targeting the rs4887091-containing enhancer reduced ADAMTS7 expression in HCASMCs (Extended Data Fig. 8f). CTCF ChIP–seq in HCASMCs demonstrated that rs4887091 overlaps a CTCF binding site (Fig. 4g). Furthermore, motif-based transcription factor binding site analysis found that rs4887091, which changes the reference (T) to alternate (C) allele, is predicted to create a core CTCF binding motif (Fig. 4h). Consistent with this prediction, haplotype-resolved CTCF ChIP–seq demonstrated allelic dosage-dependent increases in CTCF occupancy on the C allele (P = 0.0003) (Fig. 4i). Validation at control loci and orthogonal TaqMan genotyping confirmed the accuracy of the haplotype-resolved CTCF occupancy measurements (Extended Data Fig. 10h–j). Together, these data support a model in which rs4887091 creates an allele-specific CTCF binding site associated with increased local chromatin loop strength, although the effect of this loop alteration on gene expression remains to be established.

In a recent development, although our scE2G predictions are limited to enhancer–gene interactions within a cis-window, leveraging Hi-C data can link CAD GWAS variants to distal genes. For the loops present in all 15 samples, we catalogued genes linked to a CAD GWAS variant through direct chromatin contact between putative enhancers and promoters and identified 11 such genes: ANTXR1, ARMC12, CNNM2, FKBP5, CAPG, SH2D6, AMOTL2, NUAK2, RGS1, PLCL1 and FOXC2 (Fig. 5a). Among these, ANTXR1, CAPG, SH2D6, AMOTL2, NUAK2 and RGS1 are not the nearest genes. As an example, the CAD-associated variant rs9876658 was linked to AMOTL2 through a direct Hi-C contact. rs9876658 falls within a snATAC–seq peak in SMCs, endothelial cells and fibroblasts (but not myeloid cells) highlighting stroma-specific regulation (Fig. 5b). H3K27ac ChIP–seq indicated that rs9876658 overlapped a H3K27ac peak in SMCs but not in endothelial cells (Fig. 5b). Hi-ChIP–seq further identified a direct loop between the rs9876658-containing enhancer and the AMOTL2 promoter in SMCs but not in endothelial cells (Fig. 5b). Collectively, these analyses predict that the enhancer containing rs9876658 functionally regulates expression of AMOTL2 in SMCs but not in endothelial cells.

Industry observers note that a, Framework linking CAD variants to distal genes using Hi-C (left) and proportion of 15 samples containing each loop (right). Boxed genes are linked to a CAD variant by a direct Hi-C loop in all samples; red genes are non-nearest. b, LocusZoom plot for rs9876658 overlaid with human coronary Hi-C, coronary snATAC–seq and H3K27ac Hi-ChIP–seq/ChIP–seq from primary HCASMCs and HCAECs, showing an SMC-specific enhancer linked to the AMOTL2 TSS in SMCs but not in endothelial cells. P values are two-sided CAD GWAS association P values from fixed-effect inverse-variance weighted meta-analysis. c, CRISPRi of the rs9876658-containing enhancer in HCASMCs and HCAECs regulates AMOTL2 in SMCs but not in endothelial cells; non-targeting and TSS controls are shown; n = 4 biologically independent samples. Data are mean ± s.e.m.; P values were calculated using two-sided unpaired t-tests; *P < 0.05, ****P < 0.0001. d, Immunofluorescence (4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI), CNN1, ACTA2) in HCASMCs with non-targeting control or AMOTL2 knockdown. Quantification of ACTA2 and CNN1 fluorescence per DAPI+ nucleus in AMOTL2 NTC and knockdown cells across independent fields of view (n = 30). Data are mean ± s.e.m.; P values were calculated using two-sided unpaired t-tests. *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001. e, Heatmap of top differentially expressed genes in non-targeting control versus AMOTL2 knockdown in stressed HCASMCs. f, Gene ontology biological process enrichment following AMOTL2 knockdown in stressed HCASMCs. P values were calculated using one-sided Fisher’s exact tests with Benjamini–Hochberg correction. g, Violin plots of contractile genes in AMOTL2 knockdown versus control from bulk RNA-seq; n = 3 biologically independent samples. h, Cell proliferation by confluency (percentage of baseline) in control versus AMOTL2 knockdown over 72 h; n = 8 biologically independent samples; shading, mean ± s.e.m. Scale bar, 100 μm.

We found that targeting the AMOTL2 TSS led to a complete knockdown of AMOTL2 expression in HCASMCs and human coronary artery endothelial cells (HCAECs) (Fig. 5c). Importantly, targeting the rs9876658-containing enhancer reduced AMOTL2 expression in HCASMCs but not HCAECs, bolstering our prediction (Fig. 5c). Collectively, these analyses nominate rs9876658 as a causal regulator of AMOTL2 expression in SMCs but not endothelial cells and implicate this gene as a fresh candidate gene for atherosclerosis through an effect in SMCs. To dissect the functional impact of targeting AMOTL2 in HCASMCs, we compared non-targeting control and AMOTL2 knockdown HCASMCs. We observed disordered cellular morphology as well as decreased calponin (CNN1) and alpha-smooth muscle actin (ACTA2) expression by immunofluorescence in AMOTL2 knockdown cells, suggesting a shift away from the quiescent contractile state (Fig. 5d). We performed bulk RNA sequencing in stressed non-targeting control and AMOTL2 knockdown cells (Fig. 5e). Gene ontology pathway analysis revealed an upregulation of cell-cycle-related genes and a downregulation of cell-motility-associated pathways (Fig. 5f). Consistent with our immunofluorescence staining (Fig. 5d), we saw a reduction in contractile SMC gene expression (ACTA2, CNN1, TAGLN and LMOD1) in AMOTL2 knockdown cells relative to control (Fig. 5g). Finally, AMOTL2 knockdown cells had a significantly greater proliferation rate (Fig. 5h). Taken together, these findings establish a functional role for AMOTL2 in SMC proliferation and migration—pathways integral in the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis.

Although GWAS have identified hundreds of CAD-associated variants1,5,28,29, translation to therapies remains limited by incomplete understanding of the causal cell types and gene programmes30,31. The emergence of multi-omic single-cell technologies has created a unique opportunity to profile human tissue at unprecedented resolution14,32. Numerous studies have leveraged these technologies to uncover cellular heterogeneity in human tissue across many diseases, contributing to a human cell atlas17,18,24,33. Few studies have mapped common disease variants to causal cell types and target genes directly in human tissue, with previous work limited by unimodal profiling or cell-based systems that lack the native tissue context.

According to recent reports, our study used a new technique—single-nucleus multi-ome (RNA+ATAC)—in human coronary arteries from 44 patients with paired genotyping for unbiased characterization of the transcriptome and epigenome at single-cell resolution. Capturing paired gene expression and chromatin accessibility from the same nucleus allows for more robust peak-gene linkage21 and represents an notable milestone for regulatory biology of the human vasculature. We also used a new computational framework—scE2G21—to build an unbiased genome-wide scE2G map in human CAD. Notably, our scV2E2G framework identified a substantial set of CAD-associated enhancer–gene links in SMCs, including 325 linked genes, providing a basis for downstream functional interrogation of SMC regulatory programmes. This systematic approach can be applied broadly across diseases and allows for an unbiased framework to prioritize pathological genes and cell types driving common heritable human diseases.

To nominate functional regulatory variants in a broader cohort, we integrated our data with published human coronary artery snATAC–seq19 to identify 11,269 sc-caQTLs, enabling QTL discovery in cell types that are obscured in bulk analyses34,35. Mechanistic dissection of rs658956 illustrates how non-coding CAD variants can act through cell-type-specific disruption of transcription factor binding and enhancer activity36. The disruption of an AP-1 (JUN/FOS) motif by this variant is particularly notable given the well-established role of AP-1 in SMC phenotypic switching and the recent evidence that AP-1 family members act as pioneer factors governing vascular cell chromatin landscapes37 and carry epigenetic memory of inflammation38. Furthermore, SMC-specific regulation of the lncRNA FGGY-DT highlights the potential contribution of cell-restricted non-coding RNA programmes to cardiovascular disease39,40,41, although its downstream role remains to be defined.

Industry observers note that traditional pseudobulk QTL discovery lacks the ability to discriminate between molecular traits that are influenced by disease state3. Here we used single-cell genomics to define cell-state dynamics in one of the most fluid cell types in the atherosclerotic plaque. In atherosclerosis, contractile SMCs undergo de-differentiation and acquire an FMC phenotype with distinct transcriptional signatures16. We applied a continuous score reflecting SMC to FMC transition to map dynamic caQTLs that are dependent on cell-state. Using this framework, we uncovered rs658956 as a caQTL for FGGY-DT enhancer that is associated with altered activity as SMCs transition to FMCs. This is an application of single-cell-state-dependent QTL modelling in human cardiovascular disease and expands our understanding of gene regulation in heterogeneous cell states.

We applied arrayed Perturb–seq42 to GWAS-nominated enhancers and their SMC-linked target genes, enabling transcriptome-wide functional validation of non-coding regulatory elements and their downstream gene programmes. Critically, the arrayed format preserves non-cell-autonomous transcriptional effects that can be obscured in pooled screens where shared culture conditions confound intrinsic regulatory responses through paracrine signalling, as in a recent CAD variant-to-gene-to-programme framework26. The convergence of several enhancer perturbations on inflammatory and ECM-remodelling programmes is consistent with the established role of remarked processes in atherosclerosis, including induction of matrix metalloproteinases and collagens43. Together, these data support a model in which CAD variants act through cell-type-specific enhancers to co-ordinately dysregulate inflammation, ECM homeostasis and proliferation during transition from contractile SMCs to pathological FMCs18,44.

According to recent reports, given that the genome is organized as a dynamic 3D structure45, chromatin looping through topologically associating domains (TADs) represents a higher-order regulatory layer governing gene expression45,46. Although Hi-C has been used in cell-based systems and other tissues to map chromatin architecture and connect disease variants to distal genes47,48, large-scale chromatin structures are highly tissue- and cell-type-specific27,48,49 and remain unexplored in diseased human arterial tissue. Here, genome-wide Hi-C in 15 human coronary arteries enabled tissue-specific mapping of chromatin networks and distal variant–gene interactions. Notably, we discovered that rs4887091 creates an allele-specific CTCF binding site with dosage-dependent effects on both CTCF occupancy and loop strength, defining a mechanistically distinct non-coding regulatory mechanism involving 3D genome architecture48. Haplotype-resolved analysis confirmed the allele-specific increase in looping strength50,51, consistent with recent demonstrations that phased Hi-C can resolve allele-specific chromatin structure at disease loci52 and that variants within CTCF sites can alter looping and gene regulation in a dosage-sensitive manner50,51. The linked gene, ADAMTS7, is causally implicated in CAD, with Adamts7 deficiency reducing atherosclerosis and its catalytic activity regulating SMC migration53,54. Although our data do not establish altered looping as the proximal mechanism controlling ADAMTS7 expression, allele-dependent changes to chromatin architecture may represent a previously unrecognized regulatory mechanism at this locus.

According to recent reports, furthermore, our tissue Hi-C framework enabled systematic genome-wide nomination of distal causal genes. We identified 11 genes linked to CAD variants through chromatin contacts, most of which, for example AMOTL2, were not the gene nearest to the disease-associated variant. CRISPRi targeting of the enhancer linked distally to AMOTL2 reduced AMOTL2 expression in HCASMCs but not HCAECs, and AMOTL2 knockdown in HCASMCs increased cellular proliferation and suppressed contractile marker expression, consistent with a shift away from a quiescent state. This phenotype aligns with the known function of AMOTL2 as a scaffold protein55,56 that retains YAP in the cytoplasm to suppress Hippo-driven proliferative transcription, such that its loss de-represses YAP nuclear activity and promotes cell-cycle progression57. The connection between a CAD-associated variant and a Hippo pathway regulator with established roles in vascular cell proliferation and mechanosensing58,59 points to dysregulation of YAP and/or TAZ signalling in SMCs as a potentially underappreciated axis in atherosclerotic disease.

According to recent reports, our study has several limitations. First, nuclear RNA provides more limited cell-state resolution than whole-cell RNA, so we leveraged high-resolution published single-cell data for reference mapping and state imputation. Second, caQTL discovery remains constrained by sample size, cell abundance and allele frequency, limiting power in rarer cell types and variants and complicating interpretation of differences in caQTLs across cell types. Residual population stratification in our multi-ancestry cohort may have also resulted in false positives, although our summary statistics can support future meta-analyses in larger cohorts. Third, multi-ome profiling does not capture post-transcriptional regulation such as alternative splicing. Finally, bulk coronary Hi-C precludes genome-wide cell-type-specific looping inference; we therefore used targeted Hi-ChIP–seq for cell-type resolution at selected loci. Although CRISPRi Perturb–seq supports ADAMTS7 as a responsive target of the rs4887091-containing enhancer, direct allele editing or CTCF motif perturbation will be required to establish whether allele-dependent looping causally regulates ADAMTS7 expression.

In conclusion, we built a multi-omic gene-expression and chromatin-accessibility map of human CAD and provide a comprehensive framework to map CAD GWAS variants to causal genes and affected cell types. Furthermore, we use pseudobulk and single-cell QTL modelling to characterize state-dependent and independent regulatory mechanism of disease variants in human tissue. We used tissue Hi-C to build large-scale chromatin networks and uncover how disease variants impact distal gene regulation. Finally, we integrated tissue -omics with in vitro epigenetic profiling to prioritize and functionally test candidate genes using Perturb–seq and CRISPRi. Collectively, we provide a disease agnostic framework to apply human genetic findings to nominate pathologic cell states and genes driving disease, constructing a comprehensive GWAS variant-to-gene map with genetic- and tissue-level convergence for future mechanistic and therapeutic studies.

The study is compliant with all relevant ethical regulations and has been approved by the Washington University School of Medicine Institutional Review Board (no. 201104172). Informed consent was obtained from each patient before tissue collection by Washington University School of Medicine; no compensation was provided in exchange for participation in the study, and participants consented to publication of research data. Written consent was obtained. Demographic data have been de-identified and are provided in Supplementary Table 1. Patients included in this study span diverse race, age and sex to provide an inclusive trans-ethnic study population.

It has been revealed that before tissue collection, specific inclusion criteria were used to ensure well controlled study groups. Any patients with human immunodeficiency virus or hepatitis and known genetic cardiomyopathies were excluded from this study. The left anterior descending coronary artery was isolated, and flash frozen from donor hearts (patients with stable ejection fractions who experienced non-cardiac cause of death) and from patients with chronic heart failure (ischaemic and non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy) at the time of heart transplantation. For all samples, the proximal left anterior descending coronary artery was used. All demographic and clinical data have been de-identified and are provided in Supplementary Table 1. Recruitment was therefore determined by donor and/or transplant tissue availability and clinical indication rather than population-based sampling, which may limit generalizability to the broader CAD population.

Industry observers note that the left anterior descending coronary artery was dissected from explanted hearts; epicardial fat was removed, and arteries were flash frozen using liquid nitrogen. Identical regions from the proximal left anterior descending artery were used from all patients. Single-nuclei suspensions were generated as described previously17. Nuclei were isolated according to the 10x Genomics protocol (Nuclei Isolation Complex Sample for ATAC GEX Sequencing RevB, CG000375) and flow cytometry for 7-AAD (Sigma, SML1633-1ML) positive nuclei was used for sorting using a BD FACS Melody (BD Biosciences) with a 100-µm nozzle. Protocol CG000338 from 10x Genomics was used for Chromium Next GEM Single Cell Multi-ome ATAC + Gene Expression. Briefly, following nuclei isolation, permeabilization was performed, followed by transposition, GEM generation and barcoding using ChipJ (10x Genomics, PN1000234), post-GEM clean up, pre-amplification PCR, cDNA amplification, library construction and sequencing. Gene-expression and ATAC libraries were sequenced to a read depth of 50,000 and 25,000, respectively, using a NovaSeq 6000 platform (Illumina) at the McDonnell Genome Institute. Data were acquired and sorted using BD FACSChorus v.1.1.

Raw fastq files were aligned to the human GRCh38 reference genome using CellRanger ARC (10x Genomics, v.6.1), with ATAC data processed in ArchR (v.1.0.3)60 and RNA data in Seurat (v.5.5.1). After quality control, doublet removal, SCTransform normalization (sctransform v.0.4.3)61, Harmony integration (v.2.0.5)62, clustering and RNA-based cell-type annotation, RNA annotations were transferred to the paired ATAC profiles. Detailed quality control thresholds and clustering procedures are provided in Supplementary Fig. 1.

We used the scE2GMulti-ome model21 to predict enhancer–gene connections in 11 cell types from 10x Genomics multi-ome data. In each cell type, scE2G scores every candidate element–gene pair (where candidate elements are ATAC peaks within 5 Mb of the TSS of the gene) by integrating several features. Regulatory enhancer–gene interactions were defined as element–gene pairs with a score greater than 0.171.

According to recent reports, the scE2Gmulti-ome model is a supervised classifier adapted for multi-omic data from ENCODE-rE2G63. It integrates eight features, including (1) a pseudobulk activity-by-contact score, where 3D contact is estimated by an inverse function of genomic distance; (2) the Kendall correlation across single cells between element accessibility and gene expression; (3) whether the gene is ‘expressed ubiquitously’ and (4) several other measures of genomic distance and chromatin accessibility around the element and promoter. The score threshold of 0.171 was determined as the score yielding 70% recall when evaluating predictions in K562 cells against CRISPRi-validated enhancer–gene pairs.

It has been revealed that scE2G predictions for all cell types can be found in Supplementary Tables 3–14. To construct the disease-relevant scV2E2G map, we selected ATAC–seq peaks from the four main cell types that contained a CAD GWAS variant, defined cell-type-specific enhancers by overlap with coronary artery H3K27ac peaks, linked these enhancers to genes using scE2G and finally overlapped scE2G peaks with sc-caQTLs to nominate links supported by a molecular trait.

Recent findings suggest that to test for enrichment of disease risk in the four main cell types, stratified LDSC64 was used to partition heritability in cell-type marker peaks. First, cell-type specific marker peaks (FDR < 0.01, log2[fold change] > 1) were obtained using ArchR (v.1.0.3) and converted to GRCh37 coordinates using liftover65. GWAS summary statistics for CAD1, diabetes66, abdominal aortic aneurysms67, DBP and SBP68, and stroke 69 were obtained, and their formats were standardized using MungeSumstats (v.1.20.0)70. Stratified LD score analysis (LDSC v.1.0.1) was then carried out with --h2-cts flag for cell-type specific analyses. P values obtained from stratified LDSC were considered significant for a condition if they were lower than Bonferroni-corrected P value threshold of 8.33 × 10−3 (for six conditions tested). To examine overlap between CAD GWAS variants and ATAC peaks, lead variants from 241 genome-wide significant (P < 5 × 10−8) loci and 897 conditionally independent variants meeting FDR cutoff (FDR < 0.01) were obtained from Aragam and colleagues1. Additional variants that are in high linkage disequilibrium (r2 > 0.80 within 250 kb) with these lead variants were obtained from the 1000 Genomes European panel using PLINK v.1.9 --tag-r2 flag. Furthermore, these variants were combined with the functional fine-mapped credible set variants from Aragam and colleagues1 to create a superset of GWAS variants to be tested for overlap. These variants were overlapped with ATAC peak regions using the findOverlaps function in the IRanges R package (v.2.46.0).

To obtain high-quality genotypes from patients, DNA from peripheral leukocytes of 39 participants was genotyped using Illumina GSA-24-V3 SNP array. Following initial processing using Illumina GenomeStudio software v.2.0.5, variants with both (1) minor allele frequency (MAF) >5% and call rate <95% or (2) MAF <5% and call rate <99% were excluded. No patients were excluded by the call rate exclusion filter (<95%). Additional genotypes were further imputed from the TOPMED panel on the Michigan Imputation Server v.1.7.1 using minimac v.4-1.0.2 (ref. 71) and phasing with Eagle v.2.4.1 (ref. 72). Following imputation, variants with imputation R2 > 0.3 and MAF > 0.05 were further kept for caQTL analysis for a final dataset containing 7,250,405 variants. To conduct combined caQTL mapping, the variant call format (VCF) files from Turner and colleagues19 were merged with the imputed genotype dataset, and shared SNPs in only two datasets were kept for downstream analysis. Turner and colleagues carried out low-coverage whole-genome sequencing; further details are available in the original publication19. Following the merge, 5,229,397 variants were available for QTL analysis. Local ancestries were inferred using RFMix v.2.03-r0 with default settings73. Yoruba in Ibadan, Nigeria (YRI, n = 186) and Utah residents with ancestry from northern and western Europe (CEU, n = 183) from the 1000 Genomes Project74 were used as African and/or European reference populations, respectively.

To achieve uniform cell-type annotations across datasets, snATAC–seq data from Turner and colleagues19 were reference mapped onto the multi-ome dataset rather than integrated. Raw snATAC–seq data from Turner and colleagues were downloaded and reprocessed using identical quality control thresholds (minimum fragment count and TSS enrichment cut-offs) as applied to the multi-ome snATAC–seq, ensuring consistent data processing upstream of annotation. Gene activity scores were computed from the snATAC–seq data from Turner and colleagues using ArchR (v.1.0.3)60 and used as the query, with the snRNA-seq component of the multi-ome data serving as the reference for label transfer through Seurat’s anchor-based framework (v.5.5.1). This approach leveraged the higher-quality transcriptomic annotations from the multi-ome dataset to annotate the external snATAC–seq data without merging the two datasets. Annotation concordance between transferred labels and author-provided annotations from Turner and colleagues19 was assessed using Jaccard Index across the four main cell populations used for QTL mapping.

In a recent development, similar to previous studies for sc-caQTL discovery19,75, we used RASQUAL76 to identify pseudobulk caQTLs in four main cell types (SMCs, endothelial cells, myeloid cells and fibroblasts). RASQUAL v.1.1 was chosen as our mapping method due to its ability to simultaneously model allelic imbalance and count-based QTL effect to improve fine-mapping of putative causal variants. RASQUAL maximizes power for caQTL discovery by simultaneously modelling allelic imbalance and total read counts in each locus. To generate fragment counts within each ATAC peak regions, we loaded each fragment object and used Signac (v.1.17.1) FeatureMatrix function to generate a cell-by-peak count matrix for all cells within each cell type. This matrix was subsequently aggregated at a sample pseudobulk level using rollup function from the R slam package (v.0.1-56). For RASQUAL’s allele-specific modelling, createASVCF.sh script in paired-read mode was used to generate allele-specific fragment counts at each site with additional BAM flag of -F 1280 to exclude secondary or PCR duplicate reads. For each cell type, only samples with at least 20 cells of that cell type and only peaks with at least five reads on average across all samples were included for the final analysis.

Industry observers note that for the caQTL association analysis, all variants within a ±10-kb cis-window of the peaks were tested for association. Total library size for each sample was included as an offset. Age, sex, sequencing site and first four principal components of genotype data (generated from plink --pca) were included as covariates. For multiple testing correction, we used the two-step correction procedure recommended by RASQUAL76, including locus-level correction followed by a genome-wide correction using an empirical null distribution generated using genotype permutations. The caQTL variants were queried subsequently in bulk eQTL datasets using Qtlizer (v.1.22.0)77. Power, MAF-stratified validation, model comparison and genotype-PC sensitivity analyses are described in Supplementary Fig. 2. For locus-level multiple testing, a Q value corresponding to SNP-level FDR was calculated using the Benjamini–Hochberg method, and the SNP with the lowest Q value was selected for each locus. For genome-wide correction, an empirical null distribution was calculated from four RASQUAL runs using randomly permuted genotypes; the averaged null distribution was used to obtain Q value cut-offs corresponding to 1%, 5% and 10% genome-wide FDR.

We compared the myeloid cell caQTLs with previously published monocyte caQTLs discovered in peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 15 healthy donors. We found that 26.7% (767 of 2,868) of the lead macrophage caQTL variants were also the lead variant among the previously identified 3,528 monocyte caQTLs. Although only a minority, this difference may reflect the profoundly distinct biological environments between peripheral blood mononuclear cells and myeloid cells in atherosclerotic lesions75.

It has been revealed that pseudobulk caQTLs for the main cell types can be found in Supplementary Tables 15–26. To assess transcription factor binding potential at caQTLs, we trained seq2PRINT22 in SMCs using chromatin accessibility and ATAC footprinting to predict transcription factor binding probability at base-pair resolution and compared caQTL variants with non-caQTL cis-SNPs within accessible peaks.

It has been revealed that by mapping our multi-ome dataset onto a recently published coronary artery CITE-seq dataset18, we demonstrated concordant mapping scores across SMC cell states, and projecting the FMC module score into this independent dataset confirmed the score was most enriched in FMCs (Extended Data Fig. 5b–d). In human spatial transcriptomics data, the FMC score showed greater enrichment in diseased relative to healthy coronary vessels (Extended Data Fig. 5e), and in carotid plaques the FMC score correlated positively with percent stenosis (Spearman ρ = 0.58, P = 0.019), linking FMC identity directly to disease burden (Extended Data Fig. 5f). Pseudotime trajectory analysis demonstrated progressive enrichment of the FMC score as SMCs differentiate, recapitulated by both our module and an independently published gene set (Extended Data Fig. 5g,h). Using an in vitro serum starvation and replenishment model of phenotypic switching in HCASMCs followed by scRNA-seq, we confirmed that the FMC score is elevated significantly in the stressed state (Extended Data Fig. 5i). Consistent with this, published time-course murine atherosclerosis data in SMC lineage-traced cells found progressive expansion of the FMC module with disease progression (Extended Data Fig. 5j). Finally, the FMC score was correlated positively with ChromVAR-predicted activity78 of established FMC transcriptional regulators including the MEF2 family, linking chromatin remodelling to transcriptional dynamics along this differentiation axis (Extended Data Fig. 5k). Collectively, these analyses establish the reproducibility of the FMC module across independent human datasets, its association with clinical disease burden, and its relevance to both in vitro and in vivo models of SMC phenotypic switching.

In addition to the pseudobulk caQTL model, we used a PME single-cell model to map caQTLs in SMCs. This approach models cell-level fragment counts with random effect covariates to account for relatedness shared by cells from the same sample and batch. Such attempts to model discrete count distributions at a single-cell level have been shown to generally boost power in single-cell QTL discovery compared with pseudobulk and/or linear regression frameworks79,80,81. Our PME model was adapted from the PME model used by Nathan and colleagues3 for single-cell eQTL mapping as follows:.

where ATAC fragment counts (A) was modelled with fixed-effect covariates (G, genotype; nFrags, number of fragments per cell, TSSEnrich, TSS enrichment per cell; accPC, principal components of single-nucleus ATAC counts; genoPC, principal components of genotype data), random effect covariates (d, donor ID; s, sequencing site) and intercept (θ). All quantitative covariates were scaled and centred before the regression analysis. Significance of the genotype effect term (βG) was tested by LRT of the full model containing the genotype term and a null model without the genotype term. Due to the high computational load of running Poisson regression analysis on all cells, this analysis was restricted to lead caQTL variants from the pseudobulk RASQUAL analysis, which models the fragment counts using a negative binomial model. All Poisson models were fit using the glmer function from the lme4 R package (v.2.0-6). We confirmed that our data is generally not over-dispersed by plotting the mean variance relationship between a random subset of peaks. Similarly, using a zero-inflated Poisson regression model or a negative binomial model on a subset of our hits revealed little differences in overall regression estimates. Given that a small proportion of our pseudobulk hits probably represent null results, we did not conduct FDR correction due to our inability to accurately estimate the proportion of results from the null distribution. Instead, we compared z values between our pseudobulk and PME models.

A key benefit of modelling individual cells instead of sample-level pseudobulk is our ability to simultaneously model cell-state covariates (for example, differentiation trajectories, gene and/or protein expression) as well as potential interaction between genotypes and cell-state covariates. We defined FMC identity score by calculating the gene activity of the top 100 FMC (modulated SMC) marker genes defined by Wirka and colleagues16 from our integrated snATAC–seq meta-map using ArchR (v.1.0.3) addGeneScoreMatrix() and Seurat (v.5.5.1) AddModuleScore(). To test for ‘dynamic’ caQTL where the genotype effect is modified by SMC cell state, we then added the FMC score and a genotype-FMC score interaction term as covariates in the following model:.

Again, this analysis was carried out just on the significant (FDR < 5%) lead variants from the pseudobulk caQTL analyses, although it is entirely possible that there are non-significant pseudobulk caQTLs (that is, genotype effect is near zero for average FMC score) that may have significant interaction terms. We obtained P values for the genotype-FMC score interaction term using an LRT. We subsequently applied Storey Q value correction to LRT P values of the interaction term across all tested variants for multiple-testing correction. Dynamic caQTLs can be found in Supplementary Tables 29 and 30.

For EMSA, reference allele probe (5′-atagttcagaaacctgactcagccccttctt-3′) and alternate allele probe (5′- atagttcagaaaccttactcagccccttctt-3′) for rs658956 were synthesized and labelled with IRDye700 (Integrated DNA Technologies). The labelled (100 nM) and competitor (5 μM) probes were incubated with 5–10 μg of SMC nuclear extract in binding buffer (final concentration 8% Ficoll, 160 mM KCl, 20 mM HEPES, 10 mM MgCl2, 2.5 mM dithiothreitol, 0.25% Tween-20) and 1 μg of Poly dI*dC competitor at 4 °C for 1 h. For supershift assays, the protein complex was also incubated with anti-cJun (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-74543), anti-cFos (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-166940) or anti-JunB (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-8051) before addition of the probe. Following incubation, the reaction mixture was run on a 5% TBE native gel in 4 °C for 30 min to 1 h. The gel was subsequently imaged using a Bio-Rad ChemiDoc Gel Imager.

Recent findings suggest that the most effective gRNA sequence targeting an enhancer was cloned individually into the pBA904 vector and transfected into CRISPRi-HCASMC. After 5 days, RNA was collected, extracted and converted to cDNA. The effect of enhancer targeting was then assessed by comparing the expression levels of the target genes LOXL1, MYO9B, NAV1 and PALLD with that of the control. RNA was isolated using RNeasy plus micro kit (Qiagen, 74034) and total cDNA was prepared using High-capacity RNA-to-cDNA kit (Life Technologies, 4388950).

Sources indicate that parental and dCas9-Zim3 SMCs were cultured for 3 days in full medium (SmGM-2 Smooth Muscle Cell Growth Medium; Lonza, CC-3182) followed by 3 days serum starvation (base medium only) and 3 days recovery with full medium. dCas9-Zim3 SMCs were also cultured under two additional conditions for profiling: (1) 3 days full medium and (2) 3 days full medium followed by 3 days serum starvation. Cells were then processed using the Single Cell 3′ v.4 OCM kit (10x Genomics, PN-1000779) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The library was sequenced on an Illumina Nextseq2000 with read lengths (Read 1: 28, Read 2: 90, Index 1: 10, Index 2: 10). Sequencing data were demultiplexed and aligned to the human genome (GRCh38-2024-A from 10x Genomics) using CellRanger (v.9.0.1).

Library preparation was conducted with Chromium GEM-X Single Cell 3′ Reagent Kits v.4 (10x Genomics). Libraries were sequenced on NovaSeq X Plus. The initial 10x scRNA-seq dataset was processed using the CellRanger pipeline (v.8.0.0). The workflow included demultiplexing the bcl files with CellRanger mkfastq, followed by running CellRanger count using the pre-built CellRanger reference GRCh38-2020-A from 10x Genomics.

Lentivirus carrying gRNAs were produced by VectorBuilder by modifying a CROPseq vector to include a T7–U6 hybrid promoter as described previously82. Four guides were designed per TSS, three guides per enhancer region and two non-targeting controls. gRNA lentiviruses were pooled for each enhancer or TSS at a 1:1 ratio based on titre for knockdown. Cells were transfected at a multiplicity of infection of 5 and left to recover for 3 days. Puromycin (0.5 μg ml−1) was used to select for transfected cells for 4 days. Cells then underwent the 3-day starvation and 3-day recovery period as described above during which growth was monitored in an Incucyte S3 incubator and images analysed using Incucyte 2020B software. Cells were then used for single-cell transcriptomic analysis as described below.

A total of 100,000 cells from each condition were fixed with the Low Input Cell Fixation v.3 kit (Parse Biosciences, ECLC3303) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Cells were processed with the Evercode WT v.3 kit (Parse Biosciences, ECWT3300). Eight sub-libraries of 12,500 cells were generated according to manufacturer’s instructions and sequenced on an Illumina Nextseq2000 with read lengths (Read 1, 64; Read 2, 58; Index 1: 8; Index 2, 8). Sequencing data were demultiplexed and aligned to the human genome (GRCh38 Parse Biosciences) using split-pipe (v.1.6.3).

According to recent reports, raw count matrices generated by Parse Biosciences split-pipe demultiplexing were imported into R using the ReadMtx function from Seurat v.4, loading the count matrix, cell metadata and gene annotation files from the DGE_filtered directory. A Seurat object was created requiring genes detected in at least three cells and a minimum of 200 features per cell. Mitochondrial content was calculated using PercentageFeatureSet. Cells were filtered to retain those with 200–7,500 detected genes and less than 25% mitochondrial reads. Untransduced cells and two genomic coordinate-labelled perturbation conditions were excluded. Perturbation identities were mapped from sample barcodes to gene or enhancer labels, and cells were classified as non-targeting or perturbed. Gene-expression data were normalized using Seurat NormalizeData, variable features identified with FindVariableFeatures and expression values scaled with ScaleData. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed on the RNA assay, followed by UMAP embedding using the top 30 principal components.

Sources indicate that local perturbation signatures were calculated using CalcPerturbSig from Seurat, subtracting the average expression of the k = 20 nearest non-targeting neighbour cells in PCA space (30 dimensions) to remove technical variation, producing a perturbation assay. The perturbation assay was centred, projected into PCA space using variable features from the RNA assay and visualized by UMAP. Mixscape83 was run on the scaled perturbation assay using RunMixscape with a minimum of five differentially expressed genes, ten iterations and perturbation type set to knockdown. This classified cells as knockdown, escaped or non-targeting based on posterior probability of perturbation. Escaped cells were excluded from all downstream analyses. Knockdown classification rates were computed per perturbation as the proportion of cells assigned knockdown status. Linkage disequilibrium analysis was performed on knockdown and non-targeting control cells using MixscapeLDA on the PRTB assay (ten principal components, log2[fold change] threshold 0.25) and a UMAP was computed on the top linear discriminant analysis dimensions for visualization of perturbation-specific clustering.

In a recent development, differential expression between KD and non-targeting control cells was performed per perturbation using DESeq2 (v.1.52.0). Cells were assigned randomly to three pseudo-replicates within each perturbation and non-targeting control group, and raw counts were aggregated. Genes with fewer than ten total counts across pseudo-replicates were excluded. Differential expression was tested using a negative binomial model with perturbation condition as the independent variable. Results were filtered at FDR < 0.05.

It has been revealed that pre-ranked GSEA was performed per perturbation using fgsea (v.1.38.0) with genes ranked by log2[fold change] from DESeq2. Gene sets from MSigDB Hallmark and Gene Ontology Biological Process collections were obtained using the msigdbr (v.26.1.1) package (Homo sapiens). Minimum and maximum gene set sizes were set to 10 and 500, respectively, with 1,000 permutations. P values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg method across perturbations.

Pairwise cosine similarity was computed between the log2[fold change] vectors of all perturbations across the union of tested genes. Missing values were replaced with zero. Perturbations were clustered hierarchically on the resulting similarity matrix and visualized as a heatmap using pheatmap (v.1.0.13).

According to recent reports, cNMF26,84 was applied to the raw count matrix of Mixscape-classified knockdown and non-targeting control cells. Counts were exported as an AnnData h5ad file and processed using the cNMF Python package (v.1.7.1). Genes expressed in fewer than five cells and all-zero genes were removed before factorization. Factorization was performed over k = 5–10 components with 100 iterations per k value and random seed 42. The optimal k = 8 was selected based on stability and reconstruction error, with a local-density threshold of 0.01 applied during consensus clustering; 99 of 800 (12%) outlier spectra were removed. Six of eight programmes were retained based on coherent gene set enrichment; two programmes dominated by unannotated loci and lacking enrichment were excluded. cNMF usage scores were imported back into R and added to the Seurat object metadata. Programme identity was assigned by over-representation analysis of the top 100 programme-specific genes against MSigDB Hallmark and Gene Ontology Biological Process gene sets using enricher from clusterProfiler (v.4.20.0).

In a recent development, transcription factor motif enrichment per cNMF programme was assessed by over-representation analysis of top 100 programme genes against Gene Transcription Regulation Database transcription factor target-gene sets from MSigDB C3. Transcription factor activity was estimated using the univariate linear model method implemented in decoupleR (v.2.17.0), with the DoRothEA regulon85 (confidence levels A–C) as the prior network. cNMF gene specificity score vectors (genes × programmes) were used as input. Transcription factors with the highest variance across programmes were retained for visualization.

FMC module scores were computed using AddModuleScore in Seurat on a curated list of FMC marker genes as described above. Stimulated SMC up- and down-regulated gene sets were derived from FindAllMarkers differential expression between stimulated (Zim3_3d3d) and control (Zim3_ctrl) conditions, filtered at FDR < 0.05 and |log2[fold change]| > 0.25. A signed stimulation score was computed as the difference between up- and down-regulated module scores. Spearman correlations between module scores and cNMF programme usage were computed using cor.test. Per perturbation mean scores were compared using the Wilcoxon rank sum test with Benjamini–Hochberg correction. The Spearman correlation between each perturbation’s full log2[fold change] profile and the signed stimulated SMC log2[fold change] vector was computed across shared genes.

According to recent reports, RRA86 was applied across all perturbation DESeq2 gene rankings using the RobustRankAggreg (v.1.2.1) R package, separately for upregulated and down-regulated genes ranked by adjusted P value. Genes passing FDR < 0.05 after Benjamini–Hochberg correction of RRA scores were retained as the convergent programme. Each gene was assigned a direction based on the RRA result with the lower score. The top 30 convergent genes by number of perturbations in which they reached significance were selected for visualization. A convergent programme score was computed per cell as the difference between up and down module scores using AddModuleScore. Pathway enrichment of convergent up and down-regulated genes was performed using enricher against MSigDB Hallmark and GO Biological Process gene sets.

Bulk in situ Hi-C libraries for 15 different coronary artery samples across a multi-ethnic cohort were generated with the Arima Hi-C kit, according to the manufacturer’s protocols. Specifically, one Hi-C library was created from each biological sample, with an input of approximately 800,000 cells each. Restriction enzymes cutting at ^GATC and G^ANTC were used in library construction, and approximately 600 million reads were sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq 4000 per library.

It has been revealed that hi-C reads were processed with the nf-core Hi-C pipeline (v.2.0.0)87 and downstream maps were analysed at 5-kb resolution. Resolution assessment, library quality metrics, loop-caller benchmarking, inherent normalization and visualization procedures88,89 are described in Supplementary Figs. 5–7. Phased contact matrices using sample-specific genotypes were processed using Axiotl’s Turnkey platform (tinker.axiotl.com), which leverages Hi-C-Pro v.3.1.0 and cloud compute.

Industry observers note that we called cohort-specific 3D structures using the AQuA Tools framework90 for 3D genomics. Sample-wise chromatin structures were called in BEDPE format using extract_bedpe. We used union_bedpe to stack and merge BEDPE coordinates coming from various samples into one BEDPE file that contained the union set coordinates of all possible Hi-C connections in the cohort. This allowed for resolving overlapping interactions and outputting a common scaffold. To assign membership (as unique identifiers to column 7) to the stacked loops based on shared overlap of BEDPE anchors, we used cluster_bedpe. This resulting file became the mosaic for the cohort. To assess their functional and disease relevance, we intersected two-dimensional mosaic coordinates with one-dimensional genomic features including genes and snATAC peaks harbouring CAD GWAS variants. Against the mosaic BEDPE, contact values for each sample were queried in inherent and counts per million (CPM) numeric spaces using query_bedpe. All downstream analyses were performed in R.

According to recent reports, all experiments were performed on primary HCASMC between passages 4 and 7. Antibodies used for ChIP–qPCR were all pre-validated according to ChIP–seq guidelines. Purified rabbit monoclonal antibody against human CTCF (Abcam, ab128873; clone EPR7314(B)). Cell lines with various genotypes of rs4887091 were used. Approximately 2 × 106 HCASMC for each line were fixed with 1% formaldehyde and quenched by glycine. The cells were washed three times with PBS and then harvested in ChIP lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8, 5 mM EDTA, 0.5% SDS). Crosslinked chromatin was sheared for 2 × 1 min by sonication (Branson SFX250 Sonifier) before extensive centrifugation. Four volumes of ChIP dilution buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 2 mM EDTA, 1% Triton X-100) was added to the supernatant. The resulting lysate was then incubated with Dynabeads Protein G (Thermo Scientific, 10009D) and antibodies at 4 °C overnight. Beads were washed once with buffer 1 (20 mM Tris pH 8, 2 mM EDTA, 150 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 0.1% SDS), once with buffer 2 (10 mM Tris pH 8, 1 mM EDTA, 500 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 0.1% SDS), once with buffer 3 (10 mM Tris pH 8, 1 mM EDTA, 250 mM LiCl, 1% NP40, 1% sodium deoxycholate monohydrate) and twice with TE buffer. DNA was eluted by ChIP elution buffer (0.1 M NaHCO3, 1% SDS, 20 μg ml−1 proteinase K). The elution was incubated at 65 °C overnight, and DNA was extracted with a DNA purification kit (Zymo, D4013). The purified DNA from various lines were analysed by qPCR using the ABI ViiA 7, with the same primer applied to each SNP. Assays were repeated at least three times. Data are average values ± s.d. of representative experiments.

CAD-associated variants were represented as 1-bp genomic intervals (hg38) and intersected with HCASMC CTCF ChIP–seq peak intervals. Observed overlap was defined as the number of CAD variants overlapping at least one CTCF peak. To estimate overlap expected by chance while preserving genomic structure, we performed chromosome-wise circular permutation of CTCF peak coordinates. For each chromosome, peak start coordinates were shifted by a random offset uniformly sampled from \([1,L-1]\), where L is chromosome length, with wraparound at chromosome boundaries. Peak widths and chromosome assignments were preserved. For each of B = 1,000 permutations, we recalculated the number of CAD variants overlapping permuted CTCF peaks to generate an empirical null distribution.

Fold enrichment was calculated as.

Empirical one-sided P values were computed as.

For parametric approximation, we set \({p}_{0}\) to the null mean overlap probability (mean(null overlaps)/N) and computed the exact one-sided binomial probability of observing \(\ge \)k overlaps among N variants.

Sources indicate that enriched and input DNA were quantified by SYBR Green qPCR on ViiA 7. In addition to SYBR Green primers, we also used TaqMan genotyping probe (ThermoFisher, AN7EEGX, lot no. P260615-009) to directly amplify the different alleles of the DNA in heterozygous lines. Relative CTCF enrichment for target (rs4887091) and control loci was calculated as percent input. Target allele-specific binding effects were confirmed by benchmarking enrichment profiles against the expected quantitative gradients of the in-house validated allelic controls.

To identify endogenous allelic controls across the four cell lines, CTCF ChIP–seq peaks were intersected with corresponding whole-genome sequencing VCF files. SNPs exhibiting complete genotypic gradients (homozygous reference, heterozygous, homozygous alternative) were scored for CTCF motif perturbation using the JASPAR matrix (MA0139.2). Allelic positive controls were defined by severe motif disruption (\(\Delta \text{Score}\ge 6.0\), max score \( > 8.0\)), whereas negative controls exhibited preserved motif integrity (\(\Delta \text{Score}\le 0.2\), both scores \( > 8.0\)).

Recent findings suggest that to prevent cross-cell-line amplification bias, SYBR Green qPCR primers (75–150 bp amplicons) were designed using Primer3 v.2.6.1. An in silico masking pipeline strictly discarded any candidate primer pairs whose binding sites overlapped with endogenous variants in the merged four-cell-line VCF, ensuring 100% conserved annealing kinetics across all biological samples.

Industry observers note that hi-ChIP was adapted from previously published protocols with some modifications91,92. Briefly, at least 1 million healthy HCASMCs (Thermo Scientific, C-017-5C, lot no. 1689414) and healthy HCAECs (ATCC, PCS-100-020, lot no. 62382179) were crosslinked with 1% formaldehyde. The initial Hi-C portion followed the Arima Hi-C protocol described in the Arima High Coverage Hi-C Kit (Arima Genomics, A410110). For the immunoprecipitation step, sheared chromatin after the Hi-C portion of the protocol was immunoprecipitated with 5 μg of H3K27ac antibody (Abcam, ab4729) with 50 μl of protein G Dynabeads (Invitrogen 10004D) and allowed to incubate overnight at 4 °C. The protein G Dynabeads were washed and the immunoprecipitated DNA was de-crosslinked at 67 °C for 2 h and eluted (50 mM sodium bicarbonate, 1% SDS). Subsequently, Dynabeads MyOne Streptavidin C1 beads (Invitrogen, 65002) were used to enrich ligated junctions as per Hi-C protocol. Library preparation was performed using the NEB Ultra II library preparation kit (NEB, E7645L), according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Twelve PCR cycles were performed using indexed primers and subsequently DNA fragments between 300 bp and 500 bp were size selected using the Omega MagBind NGS clean up Magnetic beads (Omega, M1378). The libraries were sequenced by paired-end sequencing with at least 300 million read pairs at 2 × 151-bp read length on Illumina HiSeq 4000 platforms. Raw paired-end reads in Fastq format for respective samples were processed using the Hi-CuP pipeline93 (v.0.7.4). The hg38 human genome was used as reference to generate the Hi-CuP Digest file using two restriction motifs GATC and GANTC using the hicup_digester command for running the Hi-CuP pipeline. Paired contacts were extracted from aligned filtered bam files using Samtools (v.1.13) and used as input for the pre function in the Juicer package to generate hic files94. Paired interaction counts at 5 kb resolution were extracted from the matrix, and high-confidence chromatin loops were identified using the FitHiChIP tool (v.11.0) as described previously using default parameters95. Using HCASMC and HCAEC ChIP–seq peak files as input, and initial paired interaction files, high-confidence peak-to-all interactions with a 5-kb bin size were processed using the bash FitHiChIP_HiCPro.sh script (https://ay-lab.github.io/FitHiChIP/). High-confidence chromatin interactions were sorted and indexed in bed format and converted to long-range format for visualization on the WashU browser. The overlay of Hi-ChIP, ChIP–seq and GWAS data was plotted using the locuszoomr package (v.0.3.5) and R (v.4.3.1).

In a recent development, chIP–seq was performed as described previously with minor optimizations96. Briefly, 1 million HCASMCs and HCAECs from the same lot used for Hi-ChIP experiments were crosslinked with 1% formaldehyde for 10 min at room temperature and quenched with glycine (125 mM) for 5 min. The cells were rinsed twice with cold 1× PBS and sonicated in nuclei lysis buffer (50 mM HEPES–KOH, pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 1% Triton X, 0.1% sodium deoxycholate, 1% SDS, Takara, 1× protease inhibitor) using the Bioruptor sonicator to obtain chromatin fragments between 200 bp and 500 bp. The fragmented chromatin was immunoprecipitated overnight at 4 °C, with 5 μg of H3K27ac antibody (Abcam, ab4729) and 50 μl of protein G beads (Invitrogen, 10004D). Subsequently, the beads were washed and immunoprecipitated DNA was de-crosslinked and eluted in elution buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5, and 10 mM EDTA). Eluted ChIP fragments were isolated using phenol–chloroform extraction method, and DNA was purified by ethanol precipitation. Library preparation was performed on the eluted ChIP DNA using the NEB Ultra II library preparation kit, according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Ten PCR cycles were performed using indexed primers and the library of DNA fragments with sizes between 300 bp and 500 bp was selected using the Omega MagBind NGS clean up Magnetic beads (Omega, M1378). The libraries were sent for paired-end sequencing, with at least 50 million read pairs at 2 × 151-bp read length on the Illumina HiSeq 4000 platform. Paired-end sequencing reads were aligned to human genome (hg38) using BWA mem v.0.7.5 (ref. 97), and reads were deduplicated using Picard v.3.4.0 MarkDuplicates. Aligned mapped reads in BAM file were used as input for peak-calling using Dfilter98 to identify significant H3K27ac peaks using the following setting: -ks = 60, -bs = 100, -Ipvalue = 8. Bigwig tracks were normalized for sequencing depths and the sum of normalized binned tag-count represents the peak height.

Recent findings suggest that healthy HCASMCs (Thermo Scientific, C-017-5C, lot no. 1689414) were cultured in human vascular smooth muscle basal medium (Gibco, M231500), in Smooth Muscle Growth Supplement (Gibco, S00725) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin. Healthy HCAECs (ATCC, PCS-100-020, lot no. 62382179) were cultured in Endothelial Cell Growth medium MV2 (PromoCell, C-22022).

In a recent development, the Lentiguide-Puro plasmid was obtained as a gift from F. Zhang (Addgene, 52963, LentiGuide-Puro) in which the non-targeting control sgRNAs and sgRNAs targeting the TSS and regulatory enhancer were annealed and ligated into the Esp3I cut-site of the Lentiguide-Puro vector using T4 Ligase (NEB, M0202) as per the manufacturer’s instructions. Ligation products were transformed into One Shot Stbl3 Chemically competent Escherichia coli (Invitrogen, C737303) and plasmids of positive clones were isolated using FavorPrep Plasmid DNA Extract Kit (Favorgen, FAPDE001-1). The CRISPR interference expression vector for Lenti-dCas9-KRAB-blast (Addgene, 89567) was a gift from G. Hon. For lentivirus production, HEK293T cells were cultured in DMEM + 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) until 70% confluency before transfection. Then, 10 μg of individual plasmids, 7.5 μg of pMDLg/RRE, 2.5 μg of pRSV-Rev and 2.5 μg of pMD2.G lentivirus packaging plasmids were co-transfected with 50 μl of polyethylenimine diluted in 3 ml of Opti-MEM I Reduced Serum Medium (ThermoFisher Scientific, 31985070). Medium was refreshed overnight with reduced 5% FBS in DMEM medium, and the expended medium was collected twice after 24 h and 48 h, respectively. Pooled supernatant was filtered through a polyethersulfone 0.45 μm filter and viral particles were concentrated using Viro-PEG Lentivirus Concentrator (Ozbiosciences, LVG100) as per the manufacturer’s instructions.

At least two independent sgRNAs targeting a single regulatory element were tested against the non-targeting control. sgRNA targeting the TSS was used as positive control. Healthy HCASMCs (Thermo Scientific, C-017-5C, lot no. 1689414) and HCAECs (ATCC, PCS-100-020, lot no. 62382179) were both co-transduced in 5 μg ml−1 polybrene with lentiviral particles packaged from Lenti-dCas9-KRAB-blast (Addgene, 89567)99, and individual sgRNAs were cloned into Lentiguide-Puro backbone (Addgene, 52963)100 at a multiplicity of infection of 3. Respective HCASMC and HCAEC growth media were refreshed after 24 h of infection, and co-selection with 10 μg ml−1 blasticidin (Gibco, A1113903) and 1 μg ml−1 puromycin (Gibco, A1113803) was performed 72 h following infection. Selected cells were allowed to recover and expanded for 2 weeks before RNA isolation using Trizol Reagent (Gibco, 15596026) and Direct-Zol RNA miniprep (Zymo Research, R2052) as per the manufacturer’s instructions. cDNA conversion was performed with at least 200 ng RNA using HiScript III RT SuperMix (Vazyme Biotech, R323-01), and reverse transcription-PCR was performed using gene-specific primers to assess for gene expression.

In a recent development, cell kinetic proliferation live-cell imaging was performed using the HoloMonitor M4 system (Phase Holographic Imaging, PHI AB) using the Cell Kinetic Proliferation assay protocol as per the manufacturer’s instructions. Non-targeting controls and AMOTL2 dCas9-KRAB CRISPRi knockdown HCASMCs were seeded and cultured in vascular smooth muscle cell medium, in smooth muscle growth supplement, at a confluence of 15,000 cells cm−2 in a 24-well vessel (VWR, 734-2325) (n = 8). The 24-well HoloLid (PHI AB, 71130) was used to enhance the visualization and tracking of cells. At least five capture areas were taken per well, and time-lapse imaging at every 30-min time interval was taken across wells over 72 h. Cellular segmentation was performed using the HoloMonitor App Suite (v.3.5.2.446). Cellular confluence was captured and normalized to baseline at 0 h.

It has been revealed that total RNA was extracted using Trizol Reagent (ThermoFisher, 15596026) and Direct-Zol RNA miniprep Kit (Zymo Research, R2050). At least three independent replicates were used for RNA library preparations. RNA quality and yield was assessed using Agilent RNA 6000 pico kit (Agilent, 5067-1513) for quality. Bulk RNA-seq library preparations were prepared using VAHTS Universal V10 RNA-seq Library Prep Kit for Illumina (Vazyme, NR606-01) with Ribodepletion, according to the manufacturer’s instructions. cDNA libraries were prepared using Illumina RNA Truseq indexes and quantified using Agilent Tapestation. Sequencing was performed on the NovaSeq X Plus (PE150) by NovogeneAIT Singapore, yielding 50 million raw pair-end reads. Raw Fastq files were trimmed using the trim-galore tool (v.0.65) from Babraham Bioinformatics to sequence length of 50. Paired-end reads were mapped and aligned to the human reference genome GRCh38–hg38 using STAR aligner (v.2.7.0) as per default settings and using gene annotations from GENCODE v.38. Aligned gene counts were mapped using HTSeq-count v.2.1.2 and normalized to TPM by sequencing depth and by gene length. Differential gene-expression analysis was performed using EdgeR (v.3.42.4). Contrasts were compared between non-targeting control and AMOTL2 TSS knockdown cells. A negative binomial generalized log-linear model was used to model gene counts using the glmFit function. |log[fold change]| >0.5 and FDR < 0.05 cut-offs were used to identify significantly differentially expressed genes following multiple testing correction. Figures were generated with R v.3.5.1.

HCASMCs were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (ThermoFisher, 5090495) for 15 min at room temperature, then washed with 3× PBS for 5 min at room temperature. Cells were permeabilized with PBS with 0.1% Triton X-100 for 15 min, followed by blocking in 5% normal goat serum in PBS (blocking buffer) for 1 h at room temperature. Primary anti-Calponin (1:100) (ProteinTech, 13938-1-AP), and primary anti-α-smooth muscle actin antibody (1:100) (Sigma-Aldrich, A5228) were diluted in blocking buffer and added to permeabilized cells overnight at 4 °C. After washing with PBS three times for 5 min, cells were incubated with Alexa fluor-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:1,000) (Goat anti-mouse 594, ThermoFisher, A-11032; goat anti-rabbit 488, ThermoFisher, A-11008) and 1 μg ml−1 DAPI for 1 h at room temperature. Stained cells were washed three times for 5 min each with PBS, and images were acquired under the same laser exposure and magnification using a fluorescence microscope (EVOS M7000).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay tuned for more on these stories and anything else in or concerning Germany on November 16, 2026.

It has been revealed that we'll be back with the latest headlines out of Germany tomorrow. Bis dann!

Germany dominated neighbor and historic rival the Netherlands in their Nations League quarterfinal match-up at Berlin's Olympic Stadium on Monday evening.

It was the team's sixth game under head coach Jürgen Klopp and the 50th ever between the two sides.

In a recent development, germany's 5-0 shellacking of the Oranje was their most lopsided victory since 1959, when they won 7-0. In all, Germany have now won 19 of those matches, the Netherlands have won 12, and 18 ended in a draw.

Speaking to German broadcaster ARD after the game, attacking midfielder Florian Wirtz — who scored twice in the fixture — said: "We hope that we can make it fun for the fans. It was definitely fun for us, especially in the second half.".

Despite the loss, Xavi Hernandez's Dutch side will reach the final eight alongside Germany.

Prior to the match, Klopp had made it clear that he and his team were approaching Monday's showdown as a final after having lost to Greece 1-0 in his first home game in the job on September 27.

By night's end, Derry Scherhant and Nico Schlotterbeck each scored once and Brajan Gruda scored once and added two assists on top of Wirtz's double.

Klopp has been high on Wirtz, who has come under fire for not delivering at Liverpool since his arrival there in June 2025, and his bet seems to be paying off with the 23-year-old now scoring four goals in his last four games for Germany.

Sources indicate that "We don't care who we play. We want to play attacking football. We want to score goals and dominate the opponent. And I think we did that perfectly," stated Wirtz on Monday evening before adding: "We want to keep going next year. We want to get better. I think we've taken some great steps in our development as a team.".

A group of five EU member states, including Germany, have entered talks over a scheme to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda.

The strategy to set up so-called return hubs in a non-EU country had been announced by the group — which also includes Austria, the Netherlands, Greece and Denmark — had first been announced back in September.

Tesla has earmarked some €3 billion ($3.3 billion) to expand its factory in Germany, near to Berlin.

The Grünheide complex will be expanded to start producing the electric car organization's driverless Cybercabs, with output expected to eventually reach 1 million units.

The Elon Musk-owned company said construction would begin in 2027, with the first Cybercabs rolling off the line in 2029.

"With this, we are laying the foundations for the world's most technologically advanced Tesla factory here in Grünheide," Tesla said.

Sources indicate that germany coach Jürgen Klopp has joined the chorus of football figures critical of FIFA President Gianni Infantino. But with time running out, there are few who seem willing to run against him.

Matt Pearson on our sports desk breaks down where the power struggle right now stands, with the deadline for candiates just a matter of hours away now.

Lawmakers in the state parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania have voted in Manuela Schwesig for another term as state premier.

The 52-year-old has been in the role since 2017 and is heading into a third term.

The vote was a secret ballot, but it can still be assumed who voted and how.

She received 39 of the 68 votes cast in the chamber, exactly as many as commanded by Schwesig's three-party coaliton of her Social Democrats (29), the ecologist Greens (5), and the socialist Left Party (5).

While Söder's comments in Munich focused in particular on the policy the coalition in Berlin had not delivered, Merz initiatlly focused on talking up the efficacy of his federal coalition.

Industry observers note that "We are aware of the situation. We know that we now need to deliver. And we also know that we face difficult talks within the coalition. But I would also say from the experiences of the last weeks that there are solutions to the problems which we have in Germany," Merz said.

Merz remarked that in the 18 months since last year's election, the coalition "has already successfully implemented many things, not 'set them into motion' as people like to say, but actually implemented.".

He noted a total of 17 bills going through the second and third reading process in the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, last week, "including the most comprehensive reforms of our intelligence and security services that we have ever done in [post-war] Germany.".

Among others, he thanked Bavarian Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, a senior member of the Bavarian CSU sister party to Merz's own conservative CDU, for his contribution to this.

Merz also touted the support given to CSU politician Ilse Aigner, not just from his CDU but from the Social Democrat coalition partners and the Greens, to become the next president, calling her a person who would "represent our country very well at home and abroad.".

After hailing these accomplishments, Merz then turned to electricity tax cuts, saying he anticipated talks on the matter on Tuesday that would be "very short.".

He stated that over the weekend, coalition leaders had revisited the figures, and now believed they would be able to "completely" reduce electricity taxes to the minimum European levels in 2027 "also for private households.".

Bavarian state premier Markus Söder has appeared with Friedrich Merz at a press conference during the chancellor's trip to Munich.

It seems Söder, Merz and the CDU/CSU believe they have unfinished business after the budget was finalized in the Bundestag late last week.

Merz had pledged in the run-up to the decision to provide a reduction in electricity tax for all, but the final agreement did not include this step, with the coalition partners the Social Democrats (SPD) saying it was not adequately costed.

Söder said he and Merz had discussed "backup for the coming days," for Berlin and for a "collective stance, that is really, really key.".

He remarked the coming days were about "demonstrating credibility in politics," seemingly in reference to Merz's promise that the coalition did not ultimately deliver.

It has been revealed that "That's why it's really important to us that we do indeed bring about the reduction in electricity tax," Söder said. "This is important for businesses. It would be a relief for citizens. But it's also a matter of credibility and it's written in the coalition agreement.".

Söder said that as to the question of "where the money comes from, with a €560 billion (roughly $615 billion) budget, with €200 billion in latest debt, nobody can tell me there's no potential within the budgeting process.".

A festive piece of merchandise on the right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) "fan shop" website has upset some religious leaders in Germany.

Called a "chocolate Nicholas," it appears to depict a semblance of Saint Nicholas in bishop's regalia and the party's colors and holding a book with "AfD" written on the cover where a Bible might be in more traditional iconography.

The Bishop of Essen, Franz-Josef Overbeck, was highly critical of the promotion in Monday's edition of the Bild newspaper.

"The AfD is appropriating Christian symbols for party campaigning," Overbeck noted. "Showing the holy Nicholas in a blue coat with mitre, staff and the gospel with an AfD logo is not in order.".

Overbeck acknowledged that other organizations like football clubs would sell chocolate Christmas figurines in club colors, but he noted they would tend to refrain from including overtly Christian symbols when doing so.

Bild quoted an AfD spokesman as saying that as a "liberal-conservative party that clearly associates itself with Christian values," the item fit "particularly well" with the party image.

The main German protestant church group EKD's cultural representative, Johann Hinrich Claussen, remarked the offer indicated the AfD had "no understanding of traditions and no respect" for Christianity.

He described the action as "embarrassing and revealing," and said that Christianity was "supra-partisan.".

In a recent development, "The AfD knows little about what is holy to Christians. Otherwise, it would be aware that Bishop Nicholas of Myra, in what today is Demre in Turkey, stood clearly for uniting the occident and the orient. Beyond that, he is the patron saint of rescues at sea," Claussen mentioned.

The partner of deceased Bavarian politician Hubert Aiwanger has noted that anybody is welcome at his funeral this coming Saturday.

Aiwanger was the economy minister in Bavaria's state government as the leader of the junior coalition partners to the center-right CSU.

"Hubert was a man of the people and so it stands to reason that anyone who liked or treaasured him is allowed to come to his funeral," Tanja Schweiger wrote on her Instagram profile overnight.

She was posting after a requiem in the state capital Munich paying tribute to the leader of the Free Voters (Freie Wähler) party over the weekend. Around 1,100 people attended this ceremony.

Aiwanger died suddenly and unexpectedly on November 4 during a working visit to Berlin, aged 55.

Prosecutors have since said he died of natural causes, after he was found dead in his hotel room.

Germany's national men's football team will play neighbors and rivals the Netherlands for the 50th time on Monday night.

And there's quite a lot at stake for Jürgen Klopp's team in the last group stage game of the Nations League competition at Berlin's Olympiastadion.

If Germany win, they will qualify for the knockout stages, but a defeat could lead to potential relegation into the second tier of Nations League football.

Klopp was upbeat in the pre-match press conference at the prospect of playing the Netherlands, who he stated play "Xavi football," in the image of the skillful Spanish playmaker and World Cup winner coaching the team.

It has been revealed that "I've always loved playing against teams like this. For all my coaching career," Klopp noted. "When someone notes, 'hey they can really play football,' then in my mind the party's already started.".

According to recent reports, A full house with some 71,000 fans is expected in the capital when the game kicks off. Klopp played on the Dutch reputation for liberal use of bicylces in his comments to reporters, saying he wanted to "put a stick in their spokes" and dislodge them from the saddle.

Industry observers note that the notion of a bridge over the valley between Ratingen and Heiligenhaus to the east of Düsseldorf in western Germany as part of the A44 highway is more than half a century old. And the physical bridge itself has stood, complete, ever since 2022.

Yet still the crossing is not connected to any roads at either end.

A construction project to build the last 4.4 kilometers of highway and link the bridge to the A44 highway will formally start on Monday.

State premier Hendrik Wüst, as well as the regional transport and traffic ministers will attend the ground-breaking ceremony.

A project first conceived some 55 years ago has faced repeated delays because of lawsuits, environmental protection studies and onerous planning and permit procedures.

The bridge across the Angerbachtal (Angerbach Valley) should improve the road connection between the North Rhine-Westphalia state capital of Düsseldorf, the Bergisches Land mountain range and the industrial cities in the Ruhr Valley. It's also meant to help remove some strain from the perenially busy A3 highway and to improve the road connections to Düsseldorf International Airport.

The last stretch of highway is expected to cost around €200 million (roughly $220 million), or roughly the annual costs incurred each year by forcing traffic to divert around it, according to estimates from Düsseldorf's IHK industry and trade association.

Construction is expected to take several years, no formal end date has yet been set.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz heads to Munich early on Monday, for a meeting with the leadership of the Bavarian Christian Social Democrats (CSU), the sister party to his conservative  Christian Democrats(CDU).

No concrete details about the talks were made public ahead of time, except for the CSU saying it would serve as a general exchange that had been planned for some time.

The trip comes a week after Merz nominated Ilse Aigner as the next German president, likely paving the way for her to become the first woman and first CSU politician to assume the role.

According to recent reports, it also follows soon after the 2027 federal budget cleared a marathon meeting of the parliamentary budget committee in Berlin. This serves as one of the more conspicuous examples of the frictions and difficulties in the grand coalition between the Christian Democrats and the center-left Social Democrats — with the compromises it contains a point of frustration among the CSU and for state premier Markus Söder.

The northeastern state parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania will likely vote in Social Democrat (SPD) Manuela Schwesig for another term as state premier early in the afternoon.

The 52-year-old, who first stepped into the role in 2017, plans to lead a newly introduced coalition of the SPD, the environmentalist Greens and the socialist Left Party after state elections in September.

The right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) emerged as the largest single party in the sparsely populated state.

But still, the political calculus that emerged was arguably simpler than in Berlin — where the socialist Left Party is the largest party but could struggle to lead a coaltion — and in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD was by far the largest party but short of an outright majority.

Schwesig's SPD claimed 29 seats, with the Greens and the Left each taking 5, meaning that when combined, they hold a fairly clear majority over the AfD with its 32 seats.

Sources indicate that the SPD's relatively successful performance in the state, at least compared to its national struggles, has also led to Schwesig being linked with a possible return to federal politics. The SPD prepares to elect a newly introduced leadership duo early next year.

Schwesig has already had a spell in Berlin as the federal minsiter for families, pensioners and women, and briefly led the SPD on an interim basis in 2017, but after this she returned to her home state to seek the top regional job instead.

Servus! Welcome to another Monday of news and analysis of matters making waves in German politics and society.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz is starting his week in Munich, at a meeting of the Bavarian CSU sister party to his conservative Christian Democrats (CDU).

This comes a few days after Merz naming CSU politician Ilse Aigner as candidate to be the next president, and days after the budget committee signed off on the federal government's spending plans for 2027. Merz is expected to appear with state premier Markus Söder in a joint press conference later.

Recent findings suggest that far to the north, in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Social Democrat Manuela Schwesig should be voted in for another term as state premier in the regional parliament later in the day. Schwesig emerged in pole position after state elections a few weeks ago; some suspect her regional success could translate into national ambitions within the struggling party.

And in the west, regional leaders are headed to a road to nowhere — literally, but also hopefully not for very much longer now.

The vast highway A44 bridge over the valley between Helsinghausen and Ratingen-Ost has been planned for decades, and was completed in 2022, but work to actually connect it to the road network will only start today.

Stay with us for more on these stories and whatever else develops around Germany on November 16.
