💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers from Harvard and seven other US universities including MIT, Princeton and Yale, dominate economics prizes.Credit: Jade Gao/AFP via Getty.
  • Major prizes in economics, including the Nobel are being awarded to researchers affiliated to an increasingly concentrated set of US universities, according to a working paper published last month1.
  • Eight institutions dominate the world's top economics prizes, led Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers from Harvard and seven other US universities including MIT, Princeton and Yale, dominate economics prizes.Credit: Jade Gao/AFP via Getty.

Major prizes in economics, including the Nobel are being awarded to researchers affiliated to an increasingly concentrated set of US universities, according to a working paper published last month1.

Eight institutions dominate the world's top economics prizes, led Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

This contrasts with prizes awarded in disciplines in the natural sciences, engineering and social sciences outside economics. These have become less concentrated among certain instituions over the past 70 years, according to the working paper, which has not yet been peer reviewed.

Sources indicate that “The whole world now does science,” says Richard Freeman, an economist at Harvard University and an author on the paper, which is an update to an article presented at a National Bureau of Economic Research Summer Institute workshop in a 20242. “Our initial thought was that as the science spreads out, so too should all the prizes.” And that was the case — except in economics where “it went the other direction”.

Economist John Hassler, who is based at Stockholm University and chairs the prize-awarding committee for the Economics Prize in Memory of Alfred Nobel, states that the overall finding of concentration among a small group of US universities is not a complete surprise.

Sources indicate that “The trend is truly eye-opening and adds another dimension to the understanding of inequality within the economics profession,” adds Ashwini Deshpande, an economist at Ashoka University in Sonipat, India. “The low levels of gender, ethnic and geographic diversity within authors of top journal papers and prizes is well known and a matter of concern.”.

Freeman and his colleagues examined 171 different awards and focused their analyses on those given between 1960 and 2022, including Nobel prizes (except for literature and peace), the Fields Medal for mathematics and the Breakthrough science prizes established in 2012 by the founders of technology companies among others.

The authors of the working paper analysed the academic affiliations of the 5,859 prizewinners, working out the number of years they were linked to a specific institution. They call this metric ‘affiliation years’.

Of the 18 scientific fields of the prizewinners, 17 had a greater variety of universities represented among recipients over the time period. Economics was the outlier.

Among winners of the economics Nobel prize, seven out of 148 institutions made up 50% of affiliation years. It means that, of all the years that economics Nobel prizewinners dedicated to their discipline in academia, half of them were spent in the seven institutions.

For chemistry Nobels, 23 institutions out of 216 accounted for half of affiliation years. Twenty-six out of 243 institutions accounted for 50% of affiliation years for the physiology or medicine Nobel, and 17 out of 200 for the physics prize.

When the authors assessed all the main economics prizes between 1960 and 2022 (not only the Nobel), they found that researchers from eight out of 249 institutions represented 50% of affiliation years. In addition to Harvard, the eight are: the University of Chicago in Illinois; Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge; Stanford University in California; Princeton University in New Jersey; Yale University in New Haven, Connecticut; the University of California, Berkeley; and Columbia University in New York.

According to recent reports, by contrast, for assessed prizes in the natural sciences, 37 institutions out of 1,318 account for 50% of affiliation-years as of 2022; for engineering prizes it is 27 out of 783; and for social sciences prizes (minus economics), it is 23 out of 744. Unlike in economics, the trend for these fields is towards less concentration (see ‘Spot the outlier’).

The authors propose some possible explanations. One of these relates to another finding of the paper: “The institutions producing most of the field’s recognized work also establish the toolkit that the rest of the fields adopts,” the paper’s authors say. “Work using an unfamiliar approach is hard to place or recognize, and findings that disagree with the main tenets of the field are rejected rather than studied as special cases that may yield newly introduced knowledge.”.

Another factor, they report is that in economics, 55 per cent of Nobel laureates received the prize for a broad body of work. This contrasts somewhat with medicine and the other sciences. Some 50 per cent of prize winners in chemistry, 59 per cent in physics and 70 per cent in medicine were awarded for testable findings.

Hanzhang Zhou, a co-author on the paper and an economics doctoral candidate at MIT, claims: “When you’re giving the prize for somebody’s lifetime agenda, the institution that they’re associated with is usually one of the factors that you do take into account,” she explains.

It has been revealed that hassler told Nature that the economics prize is not intended to be a lifetime achievement award and follows the rules governing the other prize categories. He indicates it is a prize for a well-defined contribution or breakthrough, should also lead to further research in the field and that the finding must also have relevance to society at large.

French Football Federation (FFF) President Philippe Diallo has received UEFA backing to be a candidate in FIFA's presidential election, which will take place in March in Morocco, with criticism against current chief Gianni Infantino growing.

UEFA, European football's governing body, stated it has backed Diallo "unanimously" in a bid to replace Infantino, putting it's "full support" behind the Frenchman.

Veteran Japanese official Kohzo Tashima has also confirmed his candidacy, with the deadline for candidates to stand for election being November 18.

Potential candidates for the post must show letters of support from five of FIFA's 211 member associations before going through eligibility and integrity checks.

Diallo, the 63-year-old head of the FFF, is the son of a Senegalese boxing champion.

Recent findings suggest that he was elected as the federation's president in 2023 with a large majority. He was reelected for another four-year term in 2024.

Back in September, Diallo stated the FFF had withdrawn its support for Infantino ahead of the March 2027 election, saying trust in the FIFA president had "been betrayed.".

"The way in which the governance of world football is envisaged no longer reflects us," the French football head said of the decision.

If elected, the Frenchman would become FIFA's first black president, as well as it's third French leader after Robert Guerin and Jules Rimet, who served as the organization's first and third presidents.

Gianni Infantino has been in charge of world football's governing body since 2016.

Industry observers note that he has been facing growing criticism since pitching a plan of sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors. The criticism of the plan was led by UEFA and its President Aleksander Ceferin.

Infantino ended up scrapping the blueprint but UEFA went ahead and took FIFA to court in the US, trying to gather evidence ahead of potentially lodging a criminal complaint with Swiss authorities about alleged "mismanagement" by Infantino.

FIFA's headquarters are located in Zürich, Switzerland.

Infantino was also criticized after creating a peace prize and awarding it to US President Donald Trump last year.

The connection between Infantino and Trump came under criticism once again during the World Cup, after United States forward Folarin Balogun was allowed to take part in the round-of-16 game against Belgium despite having been shown a red card in the previous game.

The US president admitted to having personally intervened through a conversation with Infantino.

However, after VAR recommended an on-field review, referee Szymon Marciniak ruled the goal out for a foul on Kaique.

Patrick Dorgu was adjudged to have impeded the shot-stopper, and United subsequently had to settle for a point, leaving them 19th in the Champions League table after five matches.

As United pushed for a winning goal in Lisbon, they opted to run a trendy corner-kick routine which has increasingly become known as the 'meatwall'.

Several United players were stationed inside Sporting's six-yard box as Fernandes delivered the corner, with Dorgu, Lisandro Martinez and Leny Yoro ultimately surrounding Kaique as the ball landed in the danger zone.

Officials are supposedly attempting to clamp down on grappling and general contact from corners, in an attempt to reduce teams' reliance on scoring from set-pieces, and this policy ultimately cost United in Portugal.

Speaking on CBS Sports, former referee Christina Unkel, who is a rules expert and analyst for the American broadcaster, provided her verdict on the incident.

The ex-official claimed that those overseeing the Champions League clash at the Jose Alvalade Stadium came to the correct decision.

"Yeah, this is the right decision," she remarked.

In a recent development, "And, you know, in this match — and you guys noted there are multiple different incidents that have occurred — but this one's correct. And if you really take a look at it, there's going to be a good comparison of this one.

"You have number 13 kind of coming through and making more of the impact on that goalkeeper on the body side of it. The decision on the field, just for a reminder, was a goal, but the VAR recommended an overturn.

It has been revealed that "I think this is an appropriate overturn. Too much impact. It's coming through the side of the player, and so I think this is a good decision by the officials to take away the goal and recommend it for a foul coming out.".

It's safe to say that former Watford striker Troy Deeney, who was also on CBS Sports' panel, did not agree with Unkel's verdict.

Many felt Kaique made contact with the ball before there was any infringement from Dorgu. Deeney went a step further than this, arguing that United should have been awarded a penalty for the incident, rather than a goal.

"Goalkeepers are always protected, aren't they?" he said.

Industry observers note that "So, for me, again, he gets the advantage of being able to punch — he actually pushed it into his own goal. The penalties were all over the place.

Industry observers note that "The referee was terrible. Christina, I don't know what you thought, but watching the game, [he] kept making so many mistakes, and I thought that epitomised it. That should be a goal. Again, maybe I'm just an old fart, but that should be a goal.".

Barcelona players called for UEFA to investigate Polish referee Szymon Marciniak, who oversaw Manchester United's incident-packed Champions League encounter with Sporting CP in Lisbon on Wednesday night, back in 2025.

The official had a number of major calls to make during United's game at the Jose Alvalade Stadium. In the first half alone, Marciniak awarded Sporting two penalties, while he also disallowed a Red Devils goal from Amad Diallo.

In the second period, he handed Mauricio Pochettino's side a spot-kick before later disallowing the away team a late winner, controversially ruling out goalkeeper Kaique Pereira's own goal.

The Catalan giants lost 4-3 in northern Italy, meaning they crashed out of Europe's elite competition 7-6 on aggregate, as Inter progressed to the final.

Hansi Flick's players were incensed by a number of Marciniak's decisions during the chaotic affair, most notably when the Pole refused to award Barcelona a penalty when Inter defender Francesco Acerbi appeared to handle the ball in the box.

Acerbi struck the ball against his own hand whilst trying to clear, and VAR agreed with the referee that this couldn't be considered a punishable handling offence.

This didn't prevent Barcelona's players from feeling aggrieved, while they were also frustrated by the awarding of Inter's penalty in the first half, when Pau Cubarsi was adjudged to have fouled Lautaro Martinez.

On top of these contentious calls, Marciniak also overturned a penalty appeal when Henrikh Mkhitaryan tripped Lamine Yamal, while Barcelona also felt that there was a foul by Denzel Dumfries on Gerrard Martin in the lead-up to Acerbi's 93rd-minute equaliser.

This succession of dubious decisions prompted many Blaugrana players to take aim at the referee.

It has been revealed that pedri called for UEFA to investigate the official (via the Telegraph): “It’s not the first time that this has happened to us with this referee; UEFA should look at it. There are things that I don’t understand, and they are complicated to explain.

It has been revealed that "All 50-50s are for them. In the penalty to Lamine [Yamal], which was then a foul, he did not give Mkhitaryan a yellow card, which would have been the second.”.

Inigo Martinez chimed in: "Everyone has seen today that the decisions fell on the same side, but I don’t want this to be talked about. In the end, he [the referee] had to make decisions and he made them that way. It’s a shame.".

"We all know what happened with this refereeing team the last time we came to play in the Champions League against Inter at San Siro," Eric Garcia added.

"We have to be proud of how we competed, especially against external factors.”.

According to recent reports, barcelona's players weren't the only ones infuriated by Marciniak's performance that night at the San Siro. Spanish media were outraged, with newspaper Mundo Deportivo accusing the 45-year-old of being a 'Madridista'.

“Flick’s team overcame Inter’s initial 2-0 and the scandalous refereeing of the ‘Madridista’, who deprived Barca of a penalty for hands and whistled a very rigorous one against," - Mundo Deportivo wrote after the game.

Meanwhile, Flick was also scathing of Marciniak's display.

“Every decision that was 50-50 went [Inter’s] way," the German said.

"I am disappointed, but not with my team. I don’t like talking about the referee... I’ve told him what I think, but I’m not going to say here what I’ve said.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 07:12 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 08:10 EST, 26 November 2026.

Personal information, immigration documents and financial records have been stolen from FIFA in a cyberattack.

Football's governing body confirmed that a hacking group 'impersonated staff' to gain access to their system before taking the sensitive files.

In total, more than 12 gigabytes of data has been stolen and a group called Handsome Boy Hacking Club (HBHC) shared a screenshot of FIFA documents on X last week, claiming credit for the theft and finding access through FIFA’s Microsoft app portal.

They are understood to have then published the stolen files on a forum on the dark web, writing 'more leaks soon'.

A FIFA spokesperson noted: 'FIFA can confirm that it has been the victim of a criminal cyber-attack resulting in unauthorised access to a limited set of personal and business information.

'FIFA is working closely with the relevant authorities, including law enforcement.

FIFA were hacked and had sensitive documents stolen - pictured, FIFA president Gianni Infantino.

Handsome Boy Hacking Club took credit for the hack and shared this screenshot on X.

'FIFA condemns in the strongest possible terms the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data.

'Such actions constitute a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy and can have significant consequences for the individuals concerned.'.

According to the Athletic, immigration, financial and personal documents were stolen by the hackers impersonating staff but did not include the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), a strategy to effectively sell off the World Cup that collapsed and piled pressure on president Gianni Infantino.

The FFE plan first became public knowledge in July. Infantino sought to create a firm to manage the commercial interests of FIFA’s competitions, including the World Cup, but wanted a minority stake to be made available to private investors.

The lead investor was set to be Thrive, a firm founded by President Trump’s son-in-law’s brother, Josh Kushner, but the plan was abandoned on August 1 after three continental confederations rejected it.

It remains to be seen whether files relating to Infantino himself were taken by the hackers.

The 56-year-old is currently running for reelection against Kohzo Tashima of Japan and France football federation president Philippe Diallo.

He remains the strong favorite to win FIFA's election is held on March 18 and has already served three terms.

FIFA are the latest football-related body to have fallen victim to cyber crime, with LaLiga targeted earlier this month.

Spanish police are still investigating but LaLiga confirmed their security teams identified the source and stopped the hacker from stealing more data.

Meanwhile, a recent CaughtOffside report revealed that Liverpool are considering Verbruggen as a potential replacement for Alisson, with Chelsea and Manchester United also linked with the goalkeeper.

Standing at 6ft 4in, Verbruggen combines an imposing physical presence with impressive distribution, composure in possession and Premier League experience.

However, the suggested £60m valuation remains an estimate rather than an officially confirmed asking price.

There is little doubt that Verbruggen possesses the qualities required to become Liverpool’s first-choice goalkeeper.

At 24, he could potentially establish himself at Anfield for the next decade, while his familiarity with English football would reduce some of the risks associated with signing a goalkeeper from overseas.

However, Liverpool already have Giorgi Mamardashvili, who was recruited with the club’s long-term goalkeeping future in mind.

Spending another £60m on a goalkeeper would therefore raise legitimate questions about their recruitment strategy.

Alisson’s reported willingness to extend his stay also gives Liverpool another option.

If the Brazilian signs a upcoming contract, the Reds could afford to delay making an expensive decision regarding his successor.

Verbruggen would be an excellent signing under the right circumstances, but Liverpool must first determine whether Mamardashvili is capable of becoming their undisputed number one.

Unless serious doubts exist over the Georgian’s suitability, investing £60m elsewhere in the squad could represent a more effective use of their transfer budget.

At least show a bit more fight, a bit more quality, I can't believe I'm hearing from people who played for the club saying 4-0 is not too bad. Wow.".

The pair were both together, as usual, on the Overlap in the aftermath of that game and Neville felt he had to explain his point, leading to a bit of a heated debate.

That's what I said.

"You [Roy] remarked to them straight after that you thought it could have been eight. I thought it would have been eight. I thought it would have been eight.".

Keane, who has delivered some of football's most memorable quotes, then explained his point of view again, and could not resist a little dig at Neville in the process.

Luis Enrique was full of praise for his former club, Roma, after their 2-2 draw away against Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League on Wednesday evening, claiming that the Giallorossi have what it takes to go on and win the Serie A title and to make a deep run in Europe this season.

Roma impressed as they held the back-to-back Champions League winners to a 2-2 draw at the Parc des Princes on Wednesday night thanks to goals from Mario Hermoso and Donyell Malen, becoming the first side to take any points off PSG in the Champions League this season.

Roma have also started their Serie A season in impressive fashion: They are one of two sides that remain unbeaten after the first 12 league games of the season and are presently in second place on 30 points, two shy of league leaders and city rivals Lazio.

Enrique, whose first job in charge of a senior side came with Roma in 2011, claims that the Giallorossi could go all the way and win the Serie A title under Gian Piero Gasperini this season.

“Gasperini’s Roma is unique, they have a lot of personality and are very aggressive, we saw that from the first few minutes,” Enrique told Prime Video after full-time on Wednesday night (via Mediaset).

“They scored from their first opportunity. It was tough, a really complicated game,” he continued.

“Congratulations to Roma for the way they played, I’m happy with a point and we could have lost.

“Roma have a wonderful future ahead of them. They can go and win the Scudetto, I have no doubt that they can finish among the top 24 [in the Champions League], and I wouldn’t want to face them again. Maybe in the final.”.

While there can be little doubt about Unai Emery’s status as an elite manager in the modern game, matches at the Nou Camp continue to be the stuff of nightmares.

His record at Barcelona now reads 15 defeats from 16 matches and this was another difficult evening with Aston Villa unable to banish the demons for the man who has transformed their club.

Industry observers note that it was Emery’s 55th birthday and with the Prince of Wales and Prince George both in attendance, Villa fans were hopeful of another memorable European night. But from the moment midfielder João Gomes handed Barcelona their opening goal, it was always going to be an uphill struggle.

Emery has suffered many uncomfortable occasions at this grand old stadium, none more so than the notorious “La Remontada” of 2017 when he last competed here in the Champions League with Paris St-Germain.

This latest visit would become his heaviest defeat in Europe as Villa manager. With three wins from the opening four matches, they still have a fine chance of progressing to the knockout stage. Yet, aside from the mistakes, there will be a sense that Villa could have capitalised more against a team in the midst of a defensive injury crisis. They did have a number of chances in the first half but were left to rue their lack of ruthlessness.

According to recent reports, at the heart of Barcelona’s victory was Lamine Yamal, their outstanding jewel from the academy. The 19-year-old became the highest-scoring teenager in Champions League history, eclipsing the record of 13 he previously shared with Kylian Mbappé, with the opening goal.

Yamal was orchestrating everything from the pace of the match to the volume of the supporters, at one point imploring them to raise the noise in the first half with both arms aloft.

There was also another impressive performance from England international Anthony Gordon and Raphinha, who dedicated his two goals to the memory of Jesus de Miguel, the Tenerife forward, who died on Tuesday.

With that tragedy fresh in the minds and the Nou Camp under construction, it was a peculiar atmosphere at times.

The defeat marked the end of Villa’s 100 per cent record in the competition, with a tough test away at Galatasaray up next before they host PSG in December. They remain high up in the table and have often displayed a propensity to bounce back swiftly from defeats.

Emery said: “We are in a process and this was a very good test against a team like Barcelona. We are not at the level we want to achieve but there are a lot of experiences for us to take. Overall, we are competing fantastically in the Champions League and there is still work to do.

Sources indicate that “Over the process we’ve had here, we have made mistakes but then overcame them. We accept this defeat but take a lot of information from it.”.

Nine years have passed since Emery’s last visit in this competition and time has not proved a great healer.

Industry observers note that then in charge of PSG, Emery witnessed his team surrender a 4-0 first-leg lead to lose 6-5 on aggregate. Any matches where he is involved at the Nou Camp will revive memories of that remarkable comeback. He must have feared a repeat of more pain when Yamal, making his 37th Champions League appearance, rewarded Barcelona’s early pressure.

According to recent reports, villa’s defending needed to be as close to perfect as possible, but they were exposed after a poor error of judgment from Gomes. Under pressure from Barcelona’s attackers, Gomes panicked and played a blind pass into the path of Yamal, who bent his left-footed shot into the corner.

That mistake could have threatened to damage confidence but Villa did respond. Matty Cash’s half-volley from inside the penalty area was only a few inches wide, while Johan Manzambi side-footed wide of the goal after a quick break down the right from Nicolas Jackson.

Sources indicate that with Andreas Christensen, Eric García, Xavi Espart and Jules Koundé all absent here, Barcelona’s defence did appear vulnerable. Jackson was targeting the flanks and having his more dangerous moments challenging their high line. Emery paced his technical area, imploring his players to remain focused.

Yet Barcelona’s forward three were always a threat and they increased their lead eight minutes into the second half. Raphinha was given too much room to turn in the penalty area and his shot took a heavy deflection off the heel of Pau Torres to find the bottom corner. Emery was furious, appearing to raise his fist in the air at another poor goal conceded.

Aston Villa have made the trip over to Spain to take on Barcelona in the Champions League on matchday four. These teams last met all the way back in 1983, when they met in the European Super Cup. Barcelona won the first leg 1-0 at home before Aston Villa claimed a 3-0 victory at Villa Park, meaning Villa progressed 3-1 on aggregate.

Sources indicate that aston Villa have made the perfect start to their Champions League campaign, winning all three games, beating Club Brugge, Fenerbahce and Viking, scoring 12 goals in the process. Unai Emery’s side drew 1-1 at home against Fulham in the league on Saturday. Emery, who celebrates his 55th birthday today, has a very dismal record against Barcelona, taking just three wins from 30 matches. His last Champions League game at the Nou Camp was infamous as his PSG side lost 6-1 to go out in the last 16 back in 2017 despite winning the first leg of that tie 4-0.

“In 1982, Villa won the European Cup, and we like to think about playing in this competition again and trying to repeat that success,” Emery said. “Barcelona are favourites for what they have done in the last ten years; now they need to prove why they are favourites.

“[Barcelona] have [Lamine] Yamal. He is a special player. You can see in him as a player who could end up being the best. He needs a few things but he could end up being a great player. Rodri gives personality to the team. They have [Anthony] Gordon giving them speed and hard work. They have Pedri or Fermin [Lopez] as offensive midfielders.”.

In a recent development, barcelona started strongly in the Champions League, winning their first two games, but lost 4-2 at defending champions PSG last time out. They warmed up for this match with an emphatic 6-1 win over Alaves in La Liga on Saturday. That victory gives them a two-point lead at the summit of La Liga.

Recent findings suggest that “We know that at this level, anything can happen,” Barcelona boss Hansi Flick said. “Against Real Madrid, the result could have been different. These are special matches, but we are staying confident. It is normal to focus more on our last two defeats, but I have confidence in my team, which revealed it again on Saturday. Now, we are focused on the Champions League, with the goal of finishing in the top eight. For me, he [Unai Emery] is one of the best coaches in the world and he has reaped extraordinary successes. His team’s style of play is clear and very well organised. Just look at how they execute set pieces; it is something impressive. Their confidence in themselves is unmatched. It will be a tough match against a great team and a great coach.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that the news came on a Friday — and it was ground-shaking.
  • AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mathematics Álvaro Lozano-Robledo thought the Riemann hypothesis was out of AI’s reach for now.Credit: Bri Diaz/UConn Photo.

Recent findings suggest that the news came on a Friday — and it was ground-shaking. For months, reports have mounted of artificial-intelligence models toppling some of the toughest problems in mathematics, plunging the field into turmoil. But the latest claim was the most shocking yet: an AI model had helped to solve the field’s most famous open problem, the Riemann hypothesis.

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

The proof was released on 20 November by mathematician Levent Alpöge at AI giant Anthropic in San Francisco, California, who used an advanced version of the firm’s Claude model. It came in the form of 17 million lines of code in the open-source programming language Lean, which translates mathematical arguments into computer-certifiable code. In a matter of hours, a separate set of mathematicians rushed out a human-written proof of the Riemann hypothesis, which is in the branch of number theory and pertains to the randomness of prime numbers.

It has been revealed that alpöge’s proof has been independently verified by the non-profit organization behind Lean and the Mathlib Initiative, which runs the reference library of formalized mathematics results written in Lean. “We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him,” the community remarked in a statement on 21 November.

Sources indicate that the mathematics community has broadly accepted the claim, although responses differ wildly. Some celebrate Alpöge’s achievement, but others see the development as proof that humans are fighting against machines for the future of mathematics.

Nature hears reactions from five mathematicians on what solving the Riemann hypothesis means to them.

Mathematician Tasmin Chu is part of the Association for Human Mathematics, whose members commit to doing AI-free research.Credit: Elizabeth Xiao.

Tasmin Chu, PhD student in mathematics at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena.

A technology that can autonomously prove the Riemann hypothesis is no trivial matter. I think that it is imperative our society acts to pause AI development as soon as possible. Over the past year, mathematical institutions have faced the impossible task of adapting to the rapidly changing capabilities of AI in real time.

Industry observers note that it’s enormously disruptive for early-career researchers — the people who are the intellectual future of our field. Soon other sectors of society will face the same issues.

My reaction is grave concern. AI companies urgently require democratic oversight. I do not think AI’s encroachment into math is inevitable, nor is the death of human mathematical practice inevitable. It’s a choice to disempower ourselves, just as it’s a choice to continue building these technologies despite grave safety concerns. I continue to practice mathematics without LLMs, because I believe it’s critical that scientific inquiry continues in the hands of human beings. Some of us at the Association for Human Mathematics — whose organizing committee I am on — are collectively making the same decision.

Harini Desiraju, lecturer in mathematics at the University of Warwick, UK.

Given the events of the past few months, this news wasn't entirely a surprise, but we need to wait to understand the Lean proof and let the experts verify it. It is several million lines of code, after all.

Industry observers note that I am not a number theorist, so I might not have the same emotional attachment to the Riemann hypothesis. Nevertheless, I have deep appreciation for the ubiquity and the importance of the problem in several areas of maths and physics.

It has been revealed that as for the recent events, I want to distinguish between formal proofs versus knowledge. It is an impressive feat to solve such a problem. However, because it is a Lean proof over millions of lines, it is going to take a while before the community gets real understanding, and validity of the proof. With an AI-independent approach available as well, it could present a great opportunity for discovery of latest ideas and mathematics. We need to see how it all plays out.

Industry observers note that there is another discussion to be had, which involves the role of frontier labs in research. Most of us see the potential benefits of this technology, but it is of utmost importance that we work towards a future where the agency is with the scientific community and not a couple of companies.

Mathematician Marcus Du Sautoy is anxious about what’s next for his field.Credit: David Levenson/Getty.

Marcus Du Sautoy, mathematician and professor for the public understanding of science at the University of Oxford, UK.

Industry observers note that it was real mix of emotions. A part of me notes, how exciting to be alive when this great problem was solved! I think even when Fermat’s last theorem was solved, we had the same excitement and the same melancholy: that great motivator is gone.

Mixed in with that, is the complete surprise that it ended up being proved this way. If you’d asked me three months ago, I would never have predicted it.

There’s quite a lot of anxiety about what ‘math 2.0’ is going to look like.

Xin Zhang, assistant professor in mathematics at the University of Hong Kong.

Former US President Joe Biden's newly introduced autobiography "Promise Me, America" hit bookshelves on Tuesday, and it features anecdotes about several global leaders, including former German Chancellor Angela Merkel.

In the book, Biden dished on conversations that he and Merkel had about his predecessor and later successor, Donald Trump.

Citing conversations from early 2021, Biden wrote, "Angela was candid about her frustrations with my predecessor, who refused to shake her hand, and who seemed 'emotional' in their meetings, driven by mood swings rather than facts.".

"She also wondered," wrote Biden, "why he was 'fascinated' by Vladimir Putin and other politicians 'with autocratic and dictatorial traits.' That was a mystery I could not unravel.".

Merkel and Trump were often at odds over challenges tied to NATO, trade, climate policy and Germany's dependence on Russian energy but one of the most infamous meetings between two came in the Oval Office in March 2017, when Trump awkwardly refused to shake hands with the German leader during a press availability despite photographers loudly encouraging him to do so.

Merkel reflected on the moment in her own 2024 memoir "Freedom" saying that after initially approaching Trump as someone "completely normal" she rapidly sensed that he viewed their public meetings as a kind of "you or me" competition.

The UN's high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, has joined the chorus of those voicing doubts about a proposal by five EU countries, including Germany, to send rejected asylum seekers ​to a deportation hub ​in ‌Rwanda.

Türk remarked he had not yet ‌seen the draft proposal ‌but that ​his office was "concerned about the human rights risks raised by ​the proposed transfer of people from five ⁠European Union ​countries to ​Rwanda, where they have no ​genuine connection and ‌which has its own set ​of ⁠human rights challenges.".

Instead, he called ⁠for ​a "comprehensive approach to migration governance anchored in human rights.".

The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl noted on Tuesday that the intends would end in a "shipwreck" (see entry below).

Upcoming figures from the EU statistics agency show that just over one quarter of all students from abroad in various EU member states were enrolled in tertiary education in Germany.

Of a total of roughly 1.65 million foreign students in 2024, around 1.1 million of them were from outside the EU and the rest were moving within the EU, 438,260 were in Germany.

In a recent development, france was next in line by sheer numbers with almost 285,000 foreign students, and the much less populous Netherlands was third with over 176,000. Germany, France and the Netherlands combined accounted for more than half the bloc-wide total.

In a recent development, the Netherlands, unlike France and Germany, was also one of the countries with the highest proportion of foreign students in tertiary education. Even excluding doctoral-level students, around 18% of students in the Netherlands hailed from abroad.

Only Luxembourg, at 51.5%, Malta (35.6%), Cyprus (21.6%) and Austria (20.8%)  had a higher share among full EU members, though Switzerland's ratio also stood at roughly 20%.

Greece (2.6%), Croatia (3.5%) and Spain (4.6'%) had some of the lowest percentages of foreign students, with the EU average at 8.7%.

Mediation between German flagship carrier Lufthansa and the Vereinigung Cockpit (VC) pilots' trade union ended on Tuesday without a clear breakthrough.

The airline is trying to cut costs while the union is trying to optimize pay and conditions for members in a dispute dating back to September 2025 that led to several disruptions earlier in the year.

VC noted that it favored a package resulting from the mediation, which it said Lufthansa had rejected. VC said it was giving the airline until November 23 to reconsider its position.

Sources indicate that "The ball is now in the employer's court," VC remarked in a call with media. It did not specify what action it would take after the deadline but did say it considered its commitment not to strike during the arbitration process to be satisfied.

Lufthansa, meanwhile, remarked it had submitted a proposal to VC for up to 1,000 upcoming cockpit hires by 2033, up to 150 additional captain promotions each year, a one-off payment for 2027 and 2028 followed by salary increases from 2029 onwards.

VC noted it would be willing to make further concessions on pay and conditions if Lufthansa would respond with job guarantees.

The airline also said arbitrators had indicated a willingness to continue negotiations if the latest round proved fruitless — though it wasn't clear whether that also applied to each side of the labor dispute.

The government of the city-state of Berlin has banned an association accused of supporting the Lebanese group Hezbollah, which has been deemed a terrorist organization and outlawed in Germany since 2020.

Police in Berlin searched a total of 28 properties on Tuesday, including premises belonging to the affected groups and the homes of select members.

Recent findings suggest that the ban affects El-Irschad e.V. in the Neukölln district and three subsidiary groups: Al-Qaem e.V., Al-Thaqalyn e.V., and Qalam Bildungszentrum UG.

The city's senator, or Cabinet minister, for interior affairs, Iris Spranger of the Social Democrats, said the group was "directed against the notions of understanding between peoples," and that its "purpose and activities" contravened criminal laws in Berlin.

According to recent reports, the ban prohibits the public display or distribution of the organizations' symbols and logos. Their websites have been shut down and their assets seized.

Spranger stated the group had given Hezbollah a platform to spread propaganda among Neukölln's Shiite community, using youth activities and a mosque to do so.

A number of human rights groups have spoken out after Germany, along with Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands, announced plans to set up a hub for rejected migrants in Rwanda.

The deportation center would be the first such facility outside the European Union.

The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl mentioned on Tuesday that the prepares would end in a "shipwreck.".

Pro Asyl managing director Karl Kopp noted that even rejected asylum seekers had rights.

"Rwanda is not a model democracy. Opposition figures there are arrested and sometimes tortured," he mentioned.

"If those affected need help, we will stand at their side with legal support.".

In a statement issued after the announcement of the intends, 45 NGOs from 15 countries also condemned the move.

"These prepares allow people without a right to stay in the EU to be sent to countries with which they have no connection at all," the statement said.

"These policies shift people, and responsibility for their safety and rights, out of public sight and beyond scrutiny," it mentioned.

The junior partner in Germany's coalition, the center-left Social Democrats, has also maintained its criticism of the looks, which are heavily supported by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).

"Dobrindt's aims are short-sighted with regard to foreign policy and harm Germany's credibility," SPD foreign policy spokesman Adid Ahmetovic told the Reuters news agency.

"Rwanda violates the sovereignty of its neighbors and supports the M23 rebels in eastern [Democratic Republic of] Congo," he said.

"Such a regime must not receive any political concessions just because it is to take in refugees from Germany," he said, adding: "Human rights are not bargaining chips for deportation deals.".

The announcement of the intends comes after an EU reform of its migration policy this year granted broader detention powers and allowed for the creation of return hubs.

According to Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker, the aim is for the first center to be set up in Rwanda next year.

Diplomatic sources say the Rwanda hub will be initially run as a pilot with some 100 people, 20 from each of the five nations.

The plan to establish the deportation center in Rwanda has drawn criticism not only from a wide range of human rights groups but also from the junior partner in Germany's ruling coalition, the Social Democrats (SPD), as this video details.

Germany will be purchasing $300 million (€273 million) of US arms supplies to give to Ukraine as it fights against the Russian invasion,  German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius announced on Tuesday.

He said that Berlin was making a fifth contribution to the PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List) mechanism coordinated by the US and NATO, under which European countries finance the purchase of US weapons for Ukraine.

Most of the fresh funds will go to buy guided missiles for Patriot air defense systems, Pistorius mentioned in remarks made on the sidelines of a meeting with his EU counterparts in Brussels.

He mentioned Berlin was also planning to provide Kyiv with IRIS-T air defense systems, as previously declared, as well as new radars to improve air surveillance, ammunition for F-16 fighter jets, and drones.

He also remarked that Germany was preparing to make IRIS-T missiles compatible with NASAMS air defense systems being supplied to Ukraine by Norway.

Pistorius stressed that supporting Ukraine, although an act of solidarity, was "not a charity event," as Russian aggression posed an associated threat to Western Europe.

He is to host a meeting alongside his British counterpart Wes Streeting later on Tuesday that aims to drum up further military support for Kyiv.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has said he would like Germany to expand its relations with the former Soviet republics of Azerbaijan and Armenia as a counterweight to an ongoing bid by Russia to maintain its influence in the region.

"In the South Caucasus too, we are seeing Russia try to retain its influence at the expense of the people and their future," Wadephul on Tuesday before setting off on his first visit to the two countries as foreign minister.

He stated Russian President Vladimir Putin was opposed to countries deciding their own destiny under a European order of sovereign states, making it important for the two Caucasian nations to retain their self-determination over their futures.

Wadephul also highlighted the South Caucasus's role as an interface between Europe and Asia, which he said meant the region had great potential for trade, energy partnerships and new transport links.

Germany's top diplomat is first to visit the Azerbaijani capital, Baku, where he is set to meet the country's authoritarian head of state, Ilham Aliyev, and Foreign Minister Ceyhun Bayramov.

He is scheduled to travel on to Armenia on Wednesday.

In August 2025, the two countries signed a joint declaration on a US-brokered peace treaty ending a decadeslong conflict over the Nagorno-Karabakh region.

This came after Azerbaijan captured the region in 2023 in a short but heavy offensive, with most of the region's population — more than 100,000 ethnic Armenians — forced to flee.

Shares in Deutsche Bank took a nosedive on Tuesday after media across the world published reports with information gleaned from millions of leaked documents that expose dubious past business practices at the lender.

The documents, which were shared by unidentified whistleblowers, throw light on the banking giant's activities over the past 20 years, which include dealings with Russian oligarchs and the late convicted US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The name Donald Trump also appears in the documents from the time before he became US president.

The leaked documents, which include emails, have cast doubt on the success of chief executive Christian Sewing's efforts to turn around the institution after a series of scandals.

Among other things, they indicate that Sewing himself was involved in a working group that  sought to expand the bank's Russian operations shortly before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, despite warnings about regulatory and money-laundering risks.

The investigation, called "Inside Deutsche Bank", was conducted by over 200 journalists from a media consortium that included The Financial Times, Der Spiegel, Le Monde, the Upcoming York Times, the German public broadcaster ZDF and the Austrian daily Der Standard.

Deutsche Bank has not disputed the authenticity of the data, though it refers to the documents as "purported internal documents.".

It also said that many of the incidents referred to in them belonged to a distant past and that it is now "a different bank.".

The European Commission has almost doubled its forecast for economic growth in Germany, raising it from a prediction in spring of 0.6% to 1.3% now.

The commission stated stable domestic consumer demand and a rebound in exports justified the more optimistic figure.

The higher forecast comes despite the high inflation rate caused by the war in Iran.

Some 286,000 upcoming businesses are expected to be founded in 2026, a rise of 3.4% compared with last year and the highest level of start-ups since 2015, according to the National Association of German Cooperative Banks (BVR).

The BVR said the boom in start-ups could be partly attributed to the fact that developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and a difficult situation on the labor market were making self-employment more profitable.

However, the association warned that the increase was fragile, as it was largely driven by government support and exports rather that the private investment needed for more sustained growth.

In July, the German government adopted a start-up strategy that aimed to cut bureaucracy and provide support for future technologies, thus creating favorable conditions for young entrepreneurs.

The BVR also cautioned that the number of people in the 30-40 age group — those most likely to start a business — was falling, meaning that the surge will probably not last.

The association also stated that even though there was a rise in AI-related start-ups in 2026, Europe needed to do more for AI development to keep up with the US and China.

Footage appears to show Bruno Fernandes created the divot in the turf that led to his fortunate second goal against Sporting Lisbon.

The Manchester United captain scored a bizarre goal against his former side on Wednesday night, with his long-range shot taking a fortuitous bobble off the Estadio Jose Alvalade pitch to leave goalkeeper Kaique Pereira helpless.

While fingers were initially pointed at the ground staff, footage highlights the divot was actually created by Fernandes himself when he planted his boot into the turf while pressing high up the pitch moments earlier.

Reminiscent of former Liverpool forward Stan Collymore's famous bobbling goal past Blackburn Rovers goalkeeper Tim Flowers in 1996, Fernandes' speculative effort would undoubtedly have been easily gathered by Pereira had it not struck the bump in the turf.

The goal summed up another chaotic evening for United, in which goalkeeping calamities, controversial refereeing calls, three penalties and a red card resulted in a 2-2 draw and left them 19th in the Champions League standings.

United trailed at the break after goalkeeper Senne Lammens saved one penalty before conceding another 75 seconds later that was converted by Luis Suarez after the Belgian's reckless challenge on Max Araujo.

Fernandes' speculative effort would undoubtedly have been easily gathered by Pereira had it not struck the bump in the turf.

The visitors were left furious when Amad Diallo saw a first-half leveller ruled out after referee Szymon Marciniak blew his whistle too early for VAR to intervene, but United turned the game around shortly after the restart.

Lisandro Martinez, who had given away the first penalty, won one at the other end that Fernandes converted before the former Sporting star fired in the long-range effort that bounced over Pereira and into the net.

More drama followed as Lammens flapped at a cross under pressure from Suarez, allowing the striker to score, before Patrick Dorgu was adjudged to have put undue pressure on Pereira when forcing an own goal from the goalkeeper.

United were left frustrated by what they viewed as a lack of consistency after Marciniak was sent to the pitchside monitor to review the second decision, and their mood darkened further when Youri Tielemans was sent off for a second booking late on.

A referee accused of being drunk during an AFC Champions League Two match has released a statement regarding the allegations.

Hanna Hattab, a FIFA-licensed Syrian official, had to be replaced by fourth official Ammar Abu Alou at half-time after appearing visibly confused. Footage circulated online of the referee looking 'lost' during the match between Emirati club Al Jazira and Iranian outfit Gol Gohar.

It has been revealed that the most perplexing moment, which ultimately prompted the half-time change, came in the 32nd minute, when Hattab booked Al Jazira goalkeeper Ersin Destanoglu after a foul on Ali Asghar Ashouri in midfield. The shot-stopper was completely uninvolved, standing in his own box when the incident occurred close to the half-way line, and this unsurprisingly provoked an angry response from the Al Jazira players and coaching staff.

After several minutes of significant consultation with the assistants, the booking was rescinded.

At half-time, the Iranian giants cited this bizarre moment as a reason not to resume the match, claiming that Hattab was 'not in a normal state' and that they had seen him drinking alcohol before kick-off. The decision was then made to promote Abu Alou to oversee the second period.

After being accused of such a lack of professionalism, Hattab has broken his silence.

Releasing a statement on his Facebook page, the referee condemned those defaming his family as a result of the incident.

"A brief explanatory statement," Hattab wrote.

"Unfortunately, I am not used to that (but the wise understand from the hint).

"I will wait for the official communication and official stance from the Syrian Arab Football Federation, and I will also communicate with the people and parties responsible for me locally and internationally, before issuing an official statement that clarifies all the details and facts related to what happened in a friendly match between a Syrian and a national team in the Asian Champions League 2 yesterday, with full transparency and clarity.".

"In conclusion, I confirm that family and personal life are not the responsibility of others, and are not a game in your hands.

"Religion, reason, and morals do not tolerate the insult of people's privacy or defamation of them.

"I also confirm my full right to take all legal and judicial measures against anyone who published or made a statement or contributed to the insult and defamation of me, regardless of their position or status, whether they are an individual, an institution, or a sports entity.

"Thank you to all the good among you and the evil among them.".

Arabic sports journalist Issa Stated believes that Hattab was wrongly accused of being drunk, claiming that what happened to the official was a result of 'low blood sugar'.

"What happened to him was the result of low blood sugar, which caused him to lose focus and consciousness," Said wrote on X.

"He underwent a medical examination after the match and was not drunk, contrary to what was being circulated. I ask everyone, just as the insults and smears spread, to help spread the truth and set the record straight, and not to be the reason people lose their livelihoods and have their reputations tarnished without justification.

"Behind every name is a person, a family, and a reputation that deserves respect.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former Manchester United star Ashley Young has urged Mauricio Pochettino to make a major stance and sell Bruno Fernandes in January.

Fernandes has been a phenomenal servant to United over the years, sticking with them through thick and thin after a difficult period.

His contract, though, is set to expire next summer, though United do have the option to extend that by a further 12 months.

Reports have suggested that he has rejected two contract offers from United, but discussions have been put on hold over a fresh deal.

Fernandes clearly isn't ready to fully commit to United as they sit in the relegation zone in the Premier League.

The Portuguese international hasn't hit his usual heights so far this season, providing a goal or an assist in just two Premier League matches.

He's now looking to impress upcoming manager Mauricio Pochettino, but his future remains up in the air.

Former United player Ashley Young has suggested that Manchester United should be looking to sell Fernandes during the January transfer window.

"If Manchester United can cash in on him in January, I'd do that. I wouldn't be looking to extend his contract at all, or keep him there if he'd be unhappy. He seems to be a player for whom personal accolades are more crucial than the team, and that's what he's about. He'll be the one saying, "Yeah, I won Player of the Year. I won Player of the Year. It was me, not my other teammates." That's how he looks, and he looks that way on the pitch.".

Former Liverpool defender Stephen Warnock has suggested that it would be a 'massive stance' from Pochettino to give the green light for Fernandes to leave the club in January.

Young later tipped United to replace Fernandes with someone like Morgan Gibbs-White.

Although Fernandes has been struggling this season, he is still United's captain, which could throw a spanner in the works.

It would be a decision that wouldn't be looked at fondly by many United supporters, and we're also yet to truly see what he's like under Pochettino.

Selling Fernandes during the January transfer window would be a hugely controversial move from United.

Although many would look at the season from Fernandes and suggest he's not been at his best, he still provided 11 goals and assists in 16 games.

Last season, he hit 31 goals and assists in 37 games, so it's safe to say he's carried United on his back at times.

In fact, since joining the club, Fernandes has hit at least 20 goals and assists combined in every single season.

United won't want to lose Fernandes for free, but given they have the option to extend his contract, selling him in the middle of the campaign would certainly be a controversial move.

It'll be interesting to see how Fernandes and Pochettino work together over the coming months and whether they can drag United out of this mess.

#129815. Super subs, xG kings and $150 million question marks: The Premier League's most intriguing players

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2278 w)
📖 Baca

Super subs, xG kings and $150 million question marks: The Premier League's most intriguing players

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2278 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whatever you might think about the November international break, there is one fact you simply will not be bothered to argue against: it is well timed for the statistically-minded football fan in your life.
  • We are not yet, then, at the stage where we can always draw hard and fast conclusions.
  • Recent findings suggest that spend $100 million on a player who turns 29 next week and the expectation is surely that a player will hit the ground running.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whatever you might think about the November international break, there is one fact you simply will not be bothered to argue against: it is well timed for the statistically-minded football fan in your life. A 10-game sample size -- that's the useful stuff. At this point, many but not all teams are what their analytics tell us they are. It's similar but not quite the same for players. Not many have hit the 900-minute mark yet, but plenty are at 500-plus, a body of evidence that usually isn't warped by any one good or bad game. Of course, it depends on how good or bad that game is.

We are not yet, then, at the stage where we can always draw hard and fast conclusions. We are, however, in a position to find some interesting questions. Here are five of them, in player form:.

Recent findings suggest that spend $100 million on a player who turns 29 next week and the expectation is surely that a player will hit the ground running. That's especially true when they're Bruno Guimaraes, terror of Premier League midfields in a Newcastle United shirt, a player who had long since seemed ready to step up to a Champions League contender. While it would be fair to say that the Brazilian's form is nothing like a problem for table-topping Arsenal, he has not exactly started like a house on fire. Mikel Arteta has acknowledged as much whenever he has spoken about Guimaraes, even when served up the opportunity to praise him after what seemed an impressive performance against Hull City.

"He's hitting serious levels now, but we can still take him to another level. That's my conviction; I told him that in the dressing room -- he owned a lot of moments in the game, but there is still much more to come." It would be fair to say that, Hull aside, the best levels he has hit have been as a substitute. When he comes off the bench, he passes more accurately, wins more tackles, creates chances and scores brilliant goals. As a starter, he has occasionally looked a beat off his teammates.

Recent findings suggest that physical data from Gradient Sports hints as to what the problem might be. For every 90 Premier League minutes on the field, Guimaraes covers less of it at sprint speed (≥25 km/h) than any outfield player bar Mikel Merino and spends notably more time jogging than anyone, an average of 30 minutes. Compare Guimaraes to Declan Rice, an admittedly vertiginous bar, and it is easy to see why the new guy looks off the pace.

Equally, it explains why he's such a compelling substitute. When the other 21 players on the pitch are flagging, Guimaraes' comparative physical problems go unexposed and he can run the show.

In a recent development, that's all well and good for now, but he can't carry on like this, can he? You would have to assume that Myles Lewis-Skelly will have to make way even if the academy graduate's emergence as a midfield option unlocked an improved Declan Rice at the tail end of last season. The second most expensive signing in your history can't be an impact guy off the bench behind the homegrown kid, right? Probably not, but if there's any team that could justify the idea of Guimaraes as a 12th man, maybe it's Arsenal, where they pride themselves on their game-changing finishers.

Sources indicate that erling Haaland's Swiftian reign at the top of the Premier League xG chart has been interrupted, at least temporarily, by an unlikely source. You'd have to go back to the days of a marauding Romelu Lukaku for the last time an Everton striker looked like they might rule the roost. Only once since the Belgian's departure has an Evertonian cleared 20 goals in all competitions. In the last five, even a dozen has been beyond this club.

Sources indicate that thierno Barry isn't there yet, but boy is he on the right trajectory. His 7.28 non-penalty expected goals (npxG) puts him 0.22 ahead of Haaland and nearly 2.5 npxG up on anyone else in the league. Expand the pool to Europe's top five leagues and he is breathing rarefied air behind the top four of Lamine Yamal, Donyell Malen, Raphinha and Kylian Mbappe, all of whom have the advantage that they are not playing for an upper midtable outfit in the continent's most competitive division. And in that environment, Barry is making the hardest thing in the sport look easy: getting good shots in prime locations.

If Barry were turning them in as often as he was getting them, Everton might be even higher than sixth. Still, six goals through 10 games is not to be sniffed at, particularly when the pressure on the 24-year-old was so intense. The bungling of a deadline-day move for Folarin Balogun, as Beto moved to Fiorentina, meant it was Barry or bust for David Moyes this season.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps it was an enforced show of faith for a player who was in and out of the XI last season, his first in England, that brought the best out of the former Villarreal man. His manager views the success in more straightforward terms. "He has settled down a bit more," said Moyes after Barry's brace helped down Coventry. "His language, his understanding, his communication is much better and he has worked hard to get himself in those positions to score.".

It has been revealed that it is easy to see why getting the soft factors right might have been all that was required. Barry is the ideal striker for the modern Premier League. Tall, strong and mobile -- he ranks third among center forwards for top speed this season, per Gradient Sports -- he can serve as an outball when a press needs beating and then get in the box. He might not have the technical elegance of an Mbappe, but he makes his presence felt and occupies high-value spaces. That is more valuable than it sounds, as proven when James Tarkowski's howitzer from range deflected in off him. You might not like it, but this is what elite center forward play looks like. Long may it continue, at least as far as Everton are concerned.

There are three types of underrated footballers. First, your common-or-garden-variety underrated footballers, often to be found plying their trade at Wolverhampton Wanderers or Burnley. Ashley Westwood, in that season, put up stupidly high xA numbers. Then there are the so-often-dubbed-underrated that they actually become a bit overrated. Leighton Baines. Lee Carsley. They don't have to play for Everton, but it does help. Olivier Giroud is another. See, not all Everton.

Sources indicate that the most rarely spotted of the underrated is the chameleonic one, correctly pegged for a while, only to develop to the point that he is underrated in a completely different way to how he once was. Take Alex Iwobi. Some time ago, a consensus coalesced around the Nigeria international that he was a good player for a team at Fulham's level (and indeed Everton's). Any minute he was on the field, he would probably be delivering good performances for good Premier League teams.

According to recent reports, not anymore. Ten games in and Iwobi looks like one of the outstanding creative forces in the Premier League, critical to the march towards adequacy that Fulham have undertaken after a slow start to life with Alvaro Arbeloa.

Among true playmakers, Iwobi is one of the best at getting the ball into dangerous areas and creating for his teammates. Iwobi leads the league in expected assists with 2.95 and is tied with Bruno Fernandes for most passes completed into the penalty area. Only Pascal Gross has created more chances.

Those players can't match Iwobi when it comes to ball progression either. In terms of advancing the ball not just into the box but from deeper, Fulham's ball-playing fulcrum on the inside left channel has completed more progressive passes than anyone not named Declan Rice or Jan Paul van Hecke.

According to recent reports, when Iwobi broke through at Arsenal, he displayed a preternatural sense for how to keep attacks alive, the pass before the pass before the pass. Now a 30-year-old, Iwobi still does that more than he unpicks defenses. One cannot argue, however, that he is not putting his teammates in the right spot. It is just that not everyone quite appreciates how often he does so just yet, including his own supporters, who jeered Iwobi when he was substituted in the early-season defeat to Crystal Palace. Since then, he has responded to his critics in style, teeing up two or more shots in each of Fulham's last seven Premier League matches. If a few more of them had been converted, in fact, if any of them had been converted, then Iwobi might not still be underrated.

Sources indicate that the upper reaches of the list of most expensive transfers of all time are hardly all bangers all the time, but of the biggest money moves in the sport's history there are only a handful where at such an early stage you find yourself wondering if anyone really understood what the plan was. Manchester City committed the best part of $150 million on Enzo Fernandez this summer, a fee only eclipsed by Neymar and Kylian Mbappe. Beyond a vague sense that it would be nice to give new manager Enzo Maresca one of his favorite players, what was it they had in mind?

We pointed out earlier in the season that the aggressive positioning of Fernandez in the 5-3 win over Sunderland looked extreme; at the time it seemed reasonable to view it as a reflection of a stretched-out, chaotic game. Maresca had, of course, unlocked more number 10-ish qualities in the Argentine at Chelsea, but surely that had been reflective of what that team needed, particularly as Cole Palmer went off the boil? Perhaps not. Fernandez keeps popping up in the sort of positions that leave Elliot Anderson on an island. It is one thing to view Anderson as the newly introduced Rodri, quite another to immediately throw the England international in at the deep end, tying a whole midfield together by force of will.

Recent findings suggest that of course you could sketch out a logic for why you might push Fernandez high. It is not so long ago that City deployed two playmakers in front of a sitting midfielder and they ruled the Premier League. Fernandez and Rayan Cherki aren't Kevin De Bruyne and David Silva though.

Maybe Cherki could be offering a level of creation on a par with City greats; he started well enough last season. In year two, he is creating lower-quality chances, his expected assists per 90 dropping by 50%, notably more than the slight uptick in the quality and quantity of shots he is taking. It's no surprise that Cherki is creating less when fewer of his touches are coming in the attacking third. The output has been there so far, five goals and two assists in nine Premier League games, but for that to continue, Maresca might want to be getting his No. 10 into more dangerous spots.

Instead, those seem to be going to Fernandez, who has not proven himself able to get the final-third production to justify his platforming. For every 100 touches he takes, he is delivering significantly less npxG+xA than in either of the previous two seasons. Meanwhile, he is less effective without the ball than he has been at any stage since coming to England. That's no wonder. If an opponent passes through City's frontline, then Fernandez does not have the mobility to get back.

As such, to enable themselves to get perhaps a shot or two more than they would get with Ayyoub Bouaddi or Mateo Kovacic next to Anderson, City have made themselves an even more vulnerable side to the counterattack, already giving up more fast-break openings than they did in 2020-21 or 2021-22. Carry on like this, and Fernandez will become one of those nine-figure transfers, the ones that live in infamy.

It was a signing that delighted a city when it was unveiled in early August, and rightly so. Loaning Carl Rushworth from Brighton had been an inspired bit of business by Coventry City, the then-24-year-old goalkeeper anchoring the best defense in the division as Frank Lampard's side returned to the top flight for the first time in over a quarter of a century. A club-record £22 million fee seemed a snip for such a young talent.

All of that is worth bearing in mind given the struggles Rushworth has endured this season: saving just 53.7% of shots he has faced, conceding 5.19 more goals than the xG value of the shots he has faced. The swagger of last season has been replaced by a sloppiness apparent in both the goals he conceded in the second half against Tottenham, weak gloves doing nothing to repel efforts that came at him a bit quicker and a bit sooner than they might have last year.

None of this needs to be a problem for Rushworth. In 2023-24, James Trafford was another highly touted young goalkeeper afforded a shot at the big time by Burnley. He was obliterated up and down the Premier League, his first touch in the division picking the ball out of the net off Erling Haaland. Those struggles were the making of him, as they have broken others. It'll be some time yet before we discover which way these past few months send Rushworth.

Breaking: Could the Airbus €3 billion loan row reignite a US-EU trade dispute?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1176 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh row over a record-breaking EU loan to European aerospace company Airbus could reopen a long-standing rift with Washington and threaten an existing EU-US trade truce.
  • The European Investment Bank (EIB), the lending arm of the EU, agreed in June to loan Airbus up to €3 billion ($3.4 billion) but US President Donald Trump's top trade advisor recently suggested the loan breached a 2021 EU-US agreement on state support.
  • "I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past," US Trade Representative Jamieson Grier noted in late October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh row over a record-breaking EU loan to European aerospace company Airbus could reopen a long-standing rift with Washington and threaten an existing EU-US trade truce.

The European Investment Bank (EIB), the lending arm of the EU, agreed in June to loan Airbus up to €3 billion ($3.4 billion) but US President Donald Trump's top trade advisor recently suggested the loan breached a 2021 EU-US agreement on state support.

"I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past," US Trade Representative Jamieson Grier noted in late October. "For decades, France, Germany and Spain have aggressively supported Airbus, their national champion aircraft manufacturer, to gain an unfair advantage over US aerospace workers and business.".

In a recent development, he also suggested there was a lack of transparency around the terms of the loan. The EU insists the loan does not amount to subsidies, that it is in close contact with the Office of the US Trade Representative and "will provide all necessary information," a spokesperson told DW.

An Airbus spokesperson told DW the organization is "actively engaging with the relevant authorities and are happy to share more information about the loan with governments.".

Airbus and the US company Boeing, the world's two largest plane manufacturers, were previously involved in a 17-year corporate trade dispute.

The World Trade Organization (WTO) ruled that both the EU and US provided the companies with state subsidies, resulting in years of tariffs, tit-for-tat retaliation and claims of victory by both sides.

A deal to end tariffs with strict provisions on state support was finally agreed in 2021 and strengthened in 2025, but the latest row threatens to reopen the dispute and could potentially threaten the wider EU-US tariff deal agreed last year, experts say.

The previous Airbus-Boeing dispute was one of the longest-running corporate disputes in history and led to billions of dollars' worth of tariffs leveled by both sides.

"Trade experts tend to hate to talk about it because there are so many ups and downs to the story, it took so long to get resolved and it always tends to creep back up again," Inu Manak, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics who specializes in international trade law and policy, told DW.

Industry observers note that she claims because the glitch is such a "persistent thorn in the side," it has the potential to spiral, but for now the US is only signaling displeasure before things escalate. "They want to talk about this, and that conversation will need to happen before anything goes further," she noted.

At the heart of the current dispute is whether the €3 billion loan from the EIB, the largest corporate loan ever authorized by the bank, amounts to illegal state support.

In a recent development, "The EIB loan to Airbus is a standard loan on market terms," a European Commission spokesperson told DW. "It carries interest, it must be repaid in full, and it is the type of financing the EIB provides every year to companies across many sectors.".

A spokesperson for the bank told DW the €3 billion loan is "a standard EIB corporate loan, implemented under the bank's established procedures and on market-based terms." It claims it considers the financing to be "fully consistent with the market-terms principle" of the 2021 deal.

A spokesperson for Airbus told DW the loan is "a standard corporate financing facility, similar to commercially available loans we've signed in the past.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Fredrik Erixon, founding director of the European Center for International Political Economy, says the lines are still blurred when it comes to what counts as a subsidy and what is just a loan and that only a comprehensive World Trade Organization investigation could establish the full facts.

Another potential concern is how the €3 billion will be used, including the share earmarked for research and development and how much funding will support defense-related activities versus commercial aircraft development.

Inu Manak says it is impossible at this point to determine if the loan amounts to the provision of illegal subsidies or not, and that it depends on the very specific terms of the credit provided and whether or not it could be proved to be damaging to Boeing's business.

"If it's a market-based loan, if it's not providing below-market rates that would provide an unfair advantage, then it should be fine," she said. "That remains to be seen.".

In Erixon's view, the situation is further complicated by the fact that the aerospace sector is "a highly murky business" due to the amount of defense contracts companies like Boeing and Airbus hold with governments and the high costs associated with that in terms of research and development.

Sources indicate that "The problem is we've ended up in a world where there's only two large aircraft manufacturers," he told DW. "And it is a business with high upfront costs when you're going to develop different things.".

He points out that while Boeing may have a legitimate grievance over this loan, Airbus and the EU can point to Boeing's own deals with the US government.

"Boeing does R&D contracts for military purposes, which end up producing technology and support for the civil aircraft program for Boeing," remarked Erixon. "That's also what the World Trade Organization found previously.".

It was Boeing that originally asked the US trade representative back in July to intervene over the loan, linking it to Airbus' initiative to develop a new single-aisle aircraft program, which could spark a new era of intense competition between the two giants. Neither the US trade representative nor Boeing responded to a DW request for comment.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Inu Manak thinks the next obvious step for the US would be to launch a Section 301 investigation, which is an official inquiry to determine if the loan "violates an international trade agreement or is unjustified, unreasonable or discriminatory, and that burdens or restricts US commerce.".

She thinks the Trump administration has no interest in engaging with the WTO and believes it has the potential to threaten the broader EU-US trade agreement.

It has been revealed that "I don't think there's a lot that can stop the US trade representative from taking action if they decide they want to do it," Manak mentioned. "They may think there may be something else to extract from the European Union.".

Fredrik Erixon agrees that "it's going to be a point of leverage that the Americans can use against Europe," adding that the dynamics underpinning the aerospace sector — that both Boeing and Airbus need greater government investment due to ramped-up military spending — is the fundamental underlying problem.

"We are getting into a state aid race, which basically means these companies just need more and more and more money," he said. "That in itself is an escalatory development.".
